course.title: Psychology: How Minds Work
course.description: Detect a faint signal, watch a memory fade and recover, and test the classic studies against their replications.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with percentages, square roots and simple algebra. No previous psychology or statistics course is assumed.

paragraphs: Ask people to count the passes in a short film of a basketball game, and about half of them will fail to see a person in a gorilla suit who walks into the middle of the players, thumps their chest and walks off again. Hardly anyone who hears about the study expects to be among them, and that difference between how the mind works and how it seems to work from the inside is what psychology sets out to measure, in perception, memory, learning, judgement and the way people behave around others.

Measuring a mind is harder than measuring a beam or a star, because people differ from one another, forget, guess what a study is about and see patterns in noise. So a large part of the subject is about method, about telling a cause from a coincidence and a real effect from a lucky one, and the same reasoning lets you read a headline about sleep, screens or memory and say what the study behind it can and cannot show.

Once a finding has been measured carefully, it can usually be put into numbers that you can check for yourself. We can tell a baggage screener's skill at spotting a weapon apart from her readiness to open a bag, and the famous studies of crowds and obedience turn out to report rates that rose and fell with the details of how each study was run.
outcomes: You'll be able to say why a correlation does not show a cause and name other explanations for it.
You'll be able to judge how big a research finding is and how many people a study needs to find it.
You'll be able to separate how well someone detects a faint signal from how readily they say yes.
You'll be able to work out how likely a positive result is to be right once the base rate is counted.
You'll be able to explain how forgetting, conditioning and the pull of a crowd shape what people remember and do.

lessons.title: Correlation is not a cause

lead.text: Each dot in the figure is one day in the seaside town. How far along the bottom it sits is that day's ice-cream takings, and how high it sits is the number of pool rescues. When two measurements go up and down together across a set of cases like this, we say they are **correlated**, and because both rise together here we call it a **positive correlation**.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the second view and each dot is a person, with hours of sleep along the bottom and reaction time up the side, and the dots slope downwards. When one measure falls as the other rises we call the pattern a **negative correlation**.
Neither cloud of dots lies on a perfect line, so a correlation describes a tendency across the group and not a rule for each case.

lead.text: We'd like a single number for how tight a pattern is, one we can compare from one study to the next. That number is the **correlation coefficient**, written *r*, and it runs from −1 to +1. Its sign gives the direction, [[positive|Both measures rise together. Met on the first screen of this lesson.]] when the measures rise together and [[negative|One measure falls as the other rises. Met on the first screen of this lesson.]] when one falls as the other rises. Its size, with the sign set aside, gives the strength: **the nearer r is to 0, the weaker the pattern**, while at ±1 the dots would lie exactly on a straight line.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the town's days give r = 0.75, a fairly tight slope upwards, while hours of practice against test score give only r = 0.4, so that knowing someone's practice would help us only a *little* in guessing their score.

lead.text: A coefficient of 0.4 sounds like 40% of something, but it *isn't*, and to see what it does measure we need the idea of variation. People differ in how many hours they practise and in the scores they get, and **variation** is simply how much a measure differs from one case to the next. When two measures are correlated, some of the differences in one go along with differences in the other, and we find that **shared variation** by squaring [[r|The correlation coefficient, from −1 to +1. Met earlier in this lesson.]].

afterFigure.text: For practice and test score, r = 0.4 gives 0.4² = 0.16, so the two share 16% of their variation, and r = −0.4 would give the same 16%. The other 84% of the differences in test scores goes with everything else, such as earlier schooling, sleep, nerves and plain luck.

lead.text: Now we can answer the question we began with. Hot weather sends people to the ice-cream van and it sends them to the pool, so on a hot day takings rise and rescues rise, and on a cold day both fall. Neither list has to push on the other for the two to move together. We call a hidden factor that drives *both* measures a **confound**, and the figure colours each day by its temperature so that you can watch this one at work.

afterFigure.text: In the first view the hot days sit at the top right and the cold days at the bottom left, and that spread is the whole [[correlation|Two measures that rise and fall together across a group. Met on the first screen of this lesson.]] of 0.75. The second view keeps only the days between 21 and 23 °C. With temperature held roughly still, the dots become a shapeless cloud with a correlation near 0, so **the link between takings and rescues disappears once the confound is held fixed**. That gives us a test for any suspected confound: remove it, or hold it still, and see whether the pattern survives.

lead.text: Suppose a sample shows that people who exercise more report better moods, with r = 0.3. The tempting reading is that exercise lifts mood, but the same numbers would appear if people in a good mood were simply likelier to go out and exercise, because r treats the two measures *alike*.

afterFigure.text: When the cause runs the opposite way to the one we assumed, we call it **reverse causation**. **The numbers cannot tell the two arrows apart**, so only evidence of another kind can choose among the confound, the reverse arrow, and the arrow we first thought of.

lead.text: Not every correlation we believe in is a real one. Suppose you feel sure that it always rains after you wash your car, because you remember the soaked afternoons vividly and forget the dry ones. A fair count looks like the figure: it rained after 4 of 10 washes, and on 36 of the 90 other days.

afterFigure.text: That is 40% against 40%, so washing makes no difference, yet the memory felt like a pattern. A belief that two things go together when the counts do not support it is called an **illusory correlation**, and the remedy is to compare the *rate* in each group, not the cases that stood out. We measure the gap between two such rates in **percentage points**, so that 45% against 30% is a gap of 15 points.

blocks.text: A seaside town keeps two records through the summer: the daily takings of its ice-cream van and the number of swimmers its lifeguards pull out of the pool. Set one beside the other and they rise and fall together, so that a week of big takings is nearly always a week of many rescues.

It's tempting to say that one is behind the other, and a newspaper might well say it for you. Before agreeing, ask what *else* could produce exactly this pattern. That question is the difference between reading research on people well and being misled by it.

recap.keyIdea: A correlation tells us that two measures vary together, with a sign for the direction and a size for the strength, but it cannot tell us why.

blocks.text: A correlation coefficient *r* gives the direction and strength of a pattern, and r² gives the share of variation the two measures have in common. Behind a correlation there may be a **confound** that moves both measures, **reverse causation** that flips the arrow, or an illusory pattern that memory has built, and in each case comparing rates or holding the suspect factor still shows whether the link survives.

lessons.title: Random assignment

lead.text: Think about who signs up for a fitness programme. People who already exercise, who feel confident doing it and who have the time are the likelier ones to join, so the gym's two groups were never alike to begin with. We call this **self-selection**: the participants decided which group they would be in.

That is the [[confound|A hidden factor that drives both measures, so they correlate though neither causes the other. Met in 'Correlation is not a cause'.]] from the last lesson in a new setting. Measuring fitness more carefully can't repair this, because the trouble is not in the measuring but in *how the groups were formed*.

The cure is to take the choice away from the participants. In an **experiment** the researchers change one thing themselves and then compare groups, and what makes the comparison fair is **random assignment**: every participant has an equal chance of landing in any group, decided by something like a coin toss or names drawn from a hat. Now the keen exerciser and the reluctant one are equally likely to end up in either group, so *whatever* trait we worry about, whether exercise, motivation or money, tends to be spread evenly between them.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the same twelve people into two groups three times, using a score for their prior fitness. Each draw comes out a little differently and none is perfect, but none is *systematically* tilted towards one group. The group that receives the programme is the **treatment group**, and the group that does not is the **control group**, which shows what happens without it. Notice that random assignment is about who gets which condition, and not about how the participants were found in the first place.

lead.text: Fair does not mean identical. Suppose a draw leaves the treatment group averaging 6.5 on prior fitness and the control group 5.5, a gap of one point that nobody planned. That is an ordinary outcome of chance, and nothing has gone wrong, because what [[random assignment|Every participant has an equal chance of landing in any group. Met earlier in this lesson.]] guarantees is that **no trait is systematically more likely to favour one group**, not that two small groups will match *to the decimal*.
Chance gaps also matter less as the groups grow, because each trait has more chances to even out across the two groups, which is why researchers like larger samples.

Suppose researchers assign people [[at random|Random assignment: every participant has an equal chance of landing in any group. Met earlier in this lesson.]] to the programme or to nothing, and measure everyone's resting heart rate at the end. What the researchers set, here whether a person gets the programme, is the **independent variable**, and what they measure to see its effect, here resting heart rate, is the **dependent variable**.

'Fitness' is a *vague* idea, but 'resting heart rate in beats per minute, taken after five minutes sitting quietly' is something anyone could measure in the same way. Turning a concept into a precise, repeatable measurement gives it an **operational definition**, and that is what lets other researchers repeat a study and check it.

Even a perfectly random experiment faces a second problem, which is what people expect. Someone who takes a pill or joins a programme usually expects to improve, and expecting it can be enough to make them feel better, so a drug trial that compares a drug group with a group given nothing cannot tell the drug's effect from the effect of being treated at all.

The remedy is to give the [[control group|The group that does not receive the treatment, to show what happens without it. Met earlier in this lesson.]] a **placebo**, a pill that looks and tastes the same as the real one but has no active ingredient. Both groups now expect to improve, so the drug can be credited only with what the drug group gains *beyond* the placebo group.

Expectation can work on the researchers too, since a researcher who knows which patients got the drug may, without meaning to, give an unclear symptom the kinder rating. In a **single-blind** design only the participants are kept unaware of their condition, and in a **double-blind** design the researchers who deal with the participants and measure the outcome are kept unaware as well.

Random assignment makes the groups alike before the study, the [[placebo|A pill that looks the same as the real one but has no active ingredient. Met earlier in this lesson.]] makes their expectations alike during it, and double-blinding keeps the measuring even-handed.

blocks.text: A gym runs a twelve-week fitness programme, and at the end its records show that the members who took part are fitter than the members who didn't, so the gym would like to say that the programme made the difference.

Whether it did is the kind of question the last lesson taught us to ask of any pattern, and psychology settles such questions with a particular design, in which the researchers themselves decide who gets the programme. Once you see why that one change matters, you can look at any study that compares two groups and say whether it can show a cause or only an association.

intro.whyItMatters: A study that lets people choose their group can show only an association, while one that assigns them by chance can show a cause.

recap.keyIdea: Random assignment makes groups alike before a study begins, so that a difference afterwards can be credited to what the researchers changed.

blocks.text: When people choose their group, **self-selection** tangles whatever drove their choice into the result. In an experiment the researchers set the *independent variable*, assign people to it at random and measure the *dependent variable*, which gives every confound an equal chance of landing in either group. A placebo keeps expectation equal and a double-blind design keeps the measuring even-handed, so the difference that is left is the effect of what was changed.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll ask how big a difference has to be before it counts, and whether it would turn up again if someone repeated the study.

lessons.title: How big, and will it replicate?

lead.text: Take a class whose test scores average 60, where some score 57, some 64, a few 70 or 52. The usual measure of how widely scores are scattered around the average is the **standard deviation**, or SD, which is roughly the typical distance of a score from the average. A class whose scores usually sit about 3 points either side of 60 has an SD of about 3, and a class whose scores wander about 30 points either side has an SD of about 30.

In a bell-shaped spread of scores, **about two thirds** of people fall within one SD of the average. Beside an SD of 3, a student who scores 6 points above average is unusual, whereas beside an SD of 30 the same student is perfectly ordinary.

To compare gains across studies we divide the difference between two group averages by the [[standard deviation|Roughly the typical distance of a score from the average. Met on the previous screen.]]. The result is called **Cohen's d**, after the statistician Jacob Cohen, and it says how many standard deviations apart the groups are. In class A the course raised the average from 60 to 66 against an SD of 3, so d = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. In class B the same 6 points sits beside an SD of 30, so d = 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws each class as two bell curves, one for the untrained scores and one for the trained. In class A the curves are clearly apart, and in class B they almost coincide, although the gain in points is *identical*. Cohen offered rough labels, meant as a starting point and not a law: about 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. **A difference means little until it is measured against the spread**, and d is how we measure it.

lead.text: Real groups rarely have the same SD, so which one should we divide by? Suppose group A's scores have an SD of 2 and group B's an SD of 14. For groups of the same size the usual remedy is the **pooled standard deviation**: square each SD, average the two squares, and take the square root, which is √[(SD₁² + SD₂²) ÷ 2].

Squaring first lets the more spread-out group count for more, and that is what the data themselves do. Then [[d|Cohen's d: the difference between two group means divided by the standard deviation. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is the difference between the means divided by this pooled value.

lead.text: Chance alone produces some gap between any two groups, so researchers ask whether the gap they found is bigger than chance usually makes it. They call a result **statistically significant** when a gap that large would turn up less than 5% of the time if there were really no effect, but that says nothing yet about how *big* the effect is.

The other side of the question is **statistical power**, the chance that a study will come out significant when the effect is real. It depends on the size of the effect and on the number of people, and researchers usually aim for 80%. A small study chasing a small effect often misses an effect that exists, and when it does find one, the estimate tends to be too big, because the studies that reach significance are the ones that happened to overshoot.

How many people does a study need? A handy rule of thumb, published by Robert Lehr in 1992, says that to have 80% power at the usual 5% significance level, a two-group study needs about **16 ÷ d² people in each group**. For a medium effect, d = 0.5, that is 16 ÷ 0.25 = 64 per group. For a small effect, d = 0.2, it is 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400 per group.

afterFigure.text: Because d is squared, going from 0.5 to 0.2 makes the sample *more than six times* larger, which is why small effects are expensive to study. The rule is a rough guide for planning, and a real study would use a proper power calculation.

lead.text: Power matters most when we ask whether a finding repeats. A **replication** repeats a study with *new* participants and the same method, to see whether the result appears again. In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration attempted replications of 100 studies published in three psychology journals. Of the 97 originals that had reported a [[significant|A gap that large would arise less than 5% of the time if there were really no effect. Met earlier in this lesson.]] result, only 35 of the replications were significant, and the replications' effects averaged about half the size of the originals'.

A failure to replicate does *not* make the original researchers frauds, since low power, chance and flexible choices in the analysis explain a good deal of it. One remedy is **preregistration**, in which researchers publish their hypothesis, sample size and analysis plan before they collect any data.

Several well-known claims are now treated as cautionary cases. Carney, Cuddy and Yap (2010) reported that two minutes of expansive posing raised testosterone, and Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no such effect in 200 people. Bargh, Chen and Burrows (1996) reported that words linked to old age slowed people's walking, and Doyen and colleagues (2012) found no slowing when the walking was timed by infrared sensors.

Ego depletion is the idea that using self-control leaves less for the next task. A 2010 meta-analysis of earlier studies had put the effect near d = 0.6, and in 2016 Hagger and colleagues ran one preregistered protocol in 23 laboratories with more than 2,000 participants, and the figure shows both results on an illustrative scale.

blocks.text: A study reports that a training course raised scores by six points, and the headline calls it a big improvement. But six points has no scale attached, and whether it is big or small depends on something the headline leaves out, namely how much scores differ from person to person anyway.

Measuring a difference against that ordinary scatter is how psychologists judge the size of an effect, and once we can do it we can ask a harder question: whether a finding would turn up again if someone repeated the study.

intro.whyItMatters: Headlines rarely say how big an effect is or how many people it rests on, and those two facts decide how far to trust it.

recap.keyIdea: A difference means little until it is set against the spread of scores, and a finding means little until it has been found again.

blocks.text: Cohen's d divides the difference between two group averages by the standard deviation, using the *pooled* SD when the spreads differ, and Lehr's rule of 16 ÷ d² per group shows why small effects need large samples. Underpowered studies miss real effects and exaggerate the ones they catch, so **replication is the test that counts**, and the Open Science Collaboration's 35 successes in 97 shows how often a first result fails it.

lessons.title: Signal and noise

lead.text: Each night the guard faces two possibilities, that a thief comes or that none does, and makes one of two responses, to shout or to stay quiet, so there are four things that can happen. A shout on a thief night is a **hit**, and silence on a thief night is a **miss**. A shout on a quiet night is a **false alarm**, and silence on a quiet night is a **correct rejection**. Hits and correct rejections are the guard being right, while misses and false alarms are the two kinds of mistake, and they are different mistakes with different costs.

To compare guards we turn the counts into rates, each taken over its own kind of night. The **hit rate** is the hits divided by the number of thief nights, and the **false-alarm rate** is the false alarms divided by the number of quiet nights. Guard A, from the question you have just answered, shouted on all 10 thief nights and on 9 of the 10 quiet nights, so A's hit rate is 1.0 and A's false-alarm rate is 0.9. Guard B shouted on 8 thief nights and on 1 quiet night, so B's hit rate is 0.8 and B's false-alarm rate is 0.1. Only the *pair* of rates can tell the guards apart, because either rate alone could be had simply by shouting more or less.

A quiet night is never perfectly quiet: wind, traffic and animals make sounds that vary from one night to the next, and we call whatever is present with or without a thief the **noise**. On a thief night there is also the sound of the thief, the **signal**, which makes the night louder on average, yet a blustery quiet night can sound *louder* than a calm thief night.

afterFigure.text: Where the two curves overlap, the same loudness could have come from either kind of night, and no rule can be right every time there. The guard has to choose a loudness above which to shout, and that cut-off is the **criterion**. When the curves are far apart a criterion between them makes few mistakes, and when they are close together many nights are judged wrongly.

lead.text: Suppose the same guard decides to shout at a lower loudness. Every thief night louder than the new line now earns a shout, so the hits go up, but so does every quiet night louder than the line, so the false alarms go up too.

afterFigure.text: The hit rate and the false-alarm rate rise and fall *together*, which is why neither rate alone measures skill. What does not change when the line moves is **the distance between the two curves**, and that distance is what tells us how well the guard can tell the nights apart.

lead.text: Since the distance between the curves does not depend on where the line sits, it is the measure of skill, and it is called **d′**, read 'd prime'. It is measured in standard deviations of the noise curve: d′ = 0 means that the curves coincide and the guard cannot tell the nights apart at all, and the larger d′ is, the *easier* the nights are to tell apart.

We never see the curves, only the two rates, so we need a way back from the rates to the distance. A **z-score** says how many standard deviations a point lies from the centre of a bell curve, and every rate has a z-score: a rate of 0.50 has z = 0, rates above it have positive z-scores and rates below it negative ones, so 0.80 has z = 0.84 and 0.20 has z = −0.84. The [[false-alarm rate|False alarms divided by the number of quiet nights. Met earlier in this lesson.]] fixes how far the line lies above the centre of the noise curve, and the [[hit rate|Hits divided by the number of thief nights. Met earlier in this lesson.]] fixes how far it lies below the centre of the signal curve, so together they give the gap between the centres: **d′ = z(H) − z(FA)**, where H is the hit rate and FA the false-alarm rate.

The method came from radar engineering, where operators had to separate echoes of aircraft from clutter, and psychologists such as Wilson Tanner and John Swets brought it into the study of perception in the 1950s.

lead.text: [[d′|The distance between the noise and signal curves, d′ = z(H) − z(FA). Met earlier in this lesson.]] leaves out how ready the guard is to shout, which is the position of the line, and a convenient number for it is the **criterion location**, c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2, which measures how far the line lies from the midpoint between the two curves. A line at the midpoint gives c = 0, a guard who leans neither way. With z(H) = 0.84 and z(FA) = −0.84, for instance, c = −(0.84 − 0.84) ÷ 2 = 0.

A negative c means the guard shouts readily and collects many hits and many false alarms, while a positive c means the guard is cautious about shouting. Take a guard with z(H) = 0 and z(FA) = −1.68. Then d′ = 0 − (−1.68) = 1.68, exactly as before, but c = −(0 − 1.68) ÷ 2 = 0.84, so *the same skill* comes with a cautious line. What moves the line is what a mistake costs: a guard blamed for every theft will shout readily, one punished for every false alarm will wait to be sure, and neither change makes either of them better at hearing the thief.
At an airport a screener decides whether each bag holds a weapon, and a missed weapon costs far more than a bag opened for nothing.

blocks.text: A sound in a dark car park might be a thief at a car door, or it might be the wind, a cat or a late taxi, and the guard who hears it has to decide at once whether to shout without being able to know which. Whatever the guard decides, one of two mistakes is possible: raising the alarm for nothing, or staying quiet when a thief is there.

Judging a guard from the record of shouts seems easy, until you notice that a guard who shouts at everything catches every thief, and a guard who never shouts never raises the alarm wrongly. The record mixes together two different things, how well the guard can tell a thief from the wind and how ready the guard is to say yes.

intro.whyItMatters: Medical screening, airport security and eyewitness reports all depend on telling a real signal from noise, and on how costly each kind of mistake is.

recap.keyIdea: An observer's mistakes depend on two separate things, how far apart signal and noise lie and where the observer sets the criterion.

blocks.text: Sensitivity, d′ = z(H) − z(FA), measures how far apart the signal and noise curves lie, and the criterion location, c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2, measures where the observer sets the line. **Moving the criterion trades misses for false alarms but leaves d′ unchanged**, so two observers with very different hit rates may be equally good at the task, and only a change in the curves themselves would change that.

lessons.title: Where attention goes

lead.text: At every moment far more reaches your eyes and ears than you can make use of. What does the choosing is **selective attention**, the focusing of the mind on some things and the filtering out of the rest, and without it the stream of sensation would be overwhelming.

Selection is useful, because it lets you do one thing well, but it has a price that is easy to overlook. What the mind has not selected is not merely dimmer. It can fail to register at all, even when it is large, close and in *full view*.

In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris showed viewers a short film of two teams of three players, one in white shirts and one in black, passing basketballs. The viewers' task was to count the passes made by one of the teams. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, stopped to thump their chest, and walked out again, and when the viewers were asked afterwards, about half of them had not seen it.

People did not miss the gorilla because it was hard to see. It was on screen for several seconds, in the middle of the action. They missed it because their attention was occupied by the counting, and an object they had no reason to expect did not capture it. We call this **inattentional blindness**: a failure to notice something fully visible because attention is directed elsewhere. The lesson in it is that *looking at* something does not guarantee *seeing* it.

lead.text: Attention has a second limit, which shows up when we ask it to change jobs. In a typical task-switching experiment a person sees a pair such as 7G on every trial and is told which of two tasks to do on it: say whether the number is odd or even, or whether the letter is a vowel or a consonant. We label the two tasks A and B, so that a sequence like ABABABAB means the task changes on every trial. Whenever a trial's task differs from the one before, it is a **switch**, and the first trial of a sequence is never a switch because nothing came before it.

afterFigure.text: People are slower on a switch trial than on a trial that repeats the previous task, and the extra time is the **switch cost**. The figure uses round numbers to keep the arithmetic easy: each trial takes 500 ms and each switch adds 100 ms. In the alternating sequence the cost is paid *again and again*, while in the blocked sequence AAAABBBB it is paid only once. Stephen Monsell's review of this research in 2003 found that the cost appears across many kinds of task, and that advance warning shrinks it without usually removing it.

lead.text: Both orders in the figure on the previous screen contain the same eight trials, four of each task, so any difference in the total time comes from [[switches|A switch is a trial whose task differs from the one before. Met earlier in this lesson.]] *alone*. ABABABAB has seven switches and AAAABBBB has one, so a switch cost of 100 ms would make the blocked order 600 ms quicker.

When switches are many the costs add up, and **grouping like tasks together gives fewer of them**. Much of what people call multitasking is of this kind, a fast alternation between jobs and not two jobs done at once.

For nearly everyone doing two demanding things at once is costly. In 2010 Jason Watson and David Strayer tested 200 people who drove in a simulator while also doing a demanding mental task, and the great majority did worse when the two were combined. A handful, whom Watson and Strayer called **supertaskers**, did not.
The exceptions show that the limit is not identical in everyone, though they are rare enough that the sensible expectation for any one person is a *cost*.

What lets that little through and holds the rest back is attention, and its limits can be measured like any other. People can miss something large that passes right in front of them while their attention is busy, and every change from one task to another costs a fraction of a second, so that you can work out what a run of interruptions adds to a job and how much grouping similar tasks saves.

Only a very small share of people showed no cost from doing two demanding things at once.

lessons.title: Perception as inference

lead.text: Your senses hand you signals, and each signal is a piece of evidence about the world that is never perfectly clean. Ask your eyes to judge the height of the same block ten times, and the ten answers scatter round some typical value. We call any piece of sensory evidence that bears on a property of the world a **cue**, so the look of the block and the feel of the block are two cues to its height.

Since no cue is certain, working out what is out there means judging what is *most likely* given the evidence, and we call that process **inference**. Hermann von Helmholtz proposed in the nineteenth century that perception works in this way, and he called it unconscious inference, because it is finished before we are aware of any result.

Back to the block, with the eyes saying 50 mm and the gloved fingers saying 56 mm. Each [[cue|Any piece of sensory evidence that bears on a property of the world. Met on the previous screen.]] is noisy in its own way, and there are three obvious things to do with them. We could trust one and ignore the other, but that throws away evidence, or we could average them to 53 mm, but that treats a cue we have reason to trust exactly as it treats one we don't.

The third thing is to **lean towards the steadier cue without ignoring the other**, so that the answer is pulled towards 50 mm more than towards 56 mm, though not all the way, and what is still missing is a rule for *how far* to lean.

The rule needs a number for how steady a cue is, and we already have one: the [[standard deviation|Roughly the typical distance of a score from the average. Met in 'How big, and will it replicate?'.]] of a cue's repeated readings, small for a steady cue and large for a wobbly one. A steadier cue should *count for more*, so we turn the SD into a **reliability**, 1 ÷ SD². The square is there because the weights that give the most precise combined estimate turn out to be proportional to 1 ÷ SD², and one result is that doubling the SD cuts the reliability to a quarter, not to a half.

afterFigure.text: A cue's weight is its reliability divided by the total reliability of both cues, so the two weights add to 1, and **the combined estimate is the weighted average**: each reading multiplied by its weight, and the results added. Two cues with equal SDs get equal weights and the estimate falls at the midpoint. As one cue grows wobblier its weight falls and the estimate slides towards the other. The figure keeps the same two readings, 30 mm from sight and 36 mm from touch, and swaps which of them is the steady one.

steps.headline: Combining sight at 30 mm (SD 1) with touch at 36 mm (SD 3)

lead.text: Sight reads 30 mm with an SD of 1 mm, and touch reads 36 mm with an SD of 3 mm.

workedSteps.text: Work out each cue's reliability, 1 ÷ SD².
Divide each reliability by the total, 1 + 1/9 = 10/9, to get the two weights.
Multiply each reading by its weight and add.
The combined estimate is 30.6 mm, much nearer the steady cue's 30 mm than the midpoint, 33 mm.

lead.text: Weighting does more than choose between cues. When the two cues are independent, their [[reliabilities|A cue's reliability is 1 ÷ SD². Met earlier in this lesson.]] simply add, so the combined estimate has reliability 1 ÷ SD₁² + 1 ÷ SD₂², and its standard deviation, the **combined SD**, is one over the square root of that total. Take cues with SDs of 5 mm and 12 mm. Their reliabilities are 1/25 and 1/144, which add to 169/3600, so the combined SD is 60 ÷ 13, about 4.6 mm, *a little* better than the 5 mm of the better cue.

afterFigure.text: The second view gives two equally steady cues of 5 mm each. Their reliabilities add to 1/25 + 1/25 = 2/25, so the combined SD is √(25 ÷ 2), about 3.5 mm. Even a weak cue helps *a little*, and a second good cue helps *a lot*. In 2002 Marc Ernst and Martin Banks asked people to judge the height of a raised bar by sight, by touch and by both together, and found that the combined judgments were steadier than either sense alone, close to what this rule predicts.

lead.text: Not every cue arrives through the senses. What you expect to see is evidence as well, because it comes from everything you have seen before, and it has a [[reliability|1 ÷ SD²: how steady a cue is. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of *its own*: a firm expectation, such as that a table stands upright, has a small SD, and a vague one has a large SD. We call what you expect before the evidence arrives a **prior**, and the same rule combines it with the glimpse, weighting each by 1 ÷ SD².

afterFigure.text: In the figure you expect a line to be upright, at 0° with an SD of 2°, and the glimpse says 8°. When the glimpse is poor, with an SD of 4°, the perceived tilt is only 1.6°, and when the glimpse is clear, with an SD of 0.5°, the perceived tilt is about 7.5°. Perception shaped by knowledge and expectation, in place of being built only from the incoming features, which is called bottom-up, is **top-down processing**.

blocks.text: You pick up a small wooden block in gloves, and your fingers tell you it stands 56 mm tall. Then you look at it in good light and your eyes say 50 mm. The two readings disagree, yet you never experience two blocks, or one block of uncertain height: you perceive one block with one height, as though the matter were settled.

How does the mind get a single answer out of two that disagree? It is neither a vote nor a coin toss, and it follows a rule that we can write down and calculate. The same rule explains why a ventriloquist's voice seems to come from the dummy's mouth, and why a smudged word is easy to read in a familiar sentence and hard to read on its own.

recap.keyIdea: Perception combines cues, including what we expect, by weighting each by its reliability, and the result is steadier than any single cue.

blocks.text: Each cue is weighted by its reliability, 1 ÷ SD², and the combined estimate is the weighted average of the readings. Adding the reliabilities gives a combined SD smaller than either cue's, and an expectation can be treated as one more cue, a *prior*, which pulls what we perceive towards what we expect when the glimpse is poor. This is **top-down processing** at work, and it is one reason perception is better described as inference than as recording.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll turn to memory, beginning with how much the mind can hold at once.

lessons.title: Holding it in mind

lead.text: When you keep a phone number in mind until you can dial it, you are using **working memory**, the small workspace where information is held and used for a few seconds. It is different from **long-term memory**, the store of everything you know, which has no known limit, while the workspace has a strict one.

In 1956 George Miller put the limit at 'seven, plus or minus two' items. Later work by Nelson Cowan, reviewed in 2001, argued that when people are stopped from rehearsing and regrouping the true limit is nearer four.

Go back to the number. Read as eleven separate digits, it asks you to hold eleven things, far more than four. Read as 07700, 900 and 123, it asks for three, which fits. Miller's word for such a unit was a **chunk**: a single meaningful unit that you hold as one thing, however many items it contains. The limit counts chunks and not digits, so the same eleven digits can be a heavy load or a light one, depending on how they are grouped.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the [[store|Working memory: the small workspace where information is held and used for a few seconds. Met on the previous screen.]] with room for four chunks. With every digit separate, the digits spill far beyond it, and grouped as 5, 3 and 3 they take three slots and leave one spare. Grouping does not enlarge the store. It changes how much *each slot* holds.

lead.text: A grouping helps only when the group is something you already know, such as the habit, stored in long-term memory, of seeing a phone number as a prefix followed by two short blocks. **Chunking** is this use of what you already know to bind several items into a single chunk.

A reader who knows the acronyms FBI and NASA holds FBINASA as two chunks, whereas a reader who knows neither has to hold seven separate letters. The capacity of working memory is *the same* for both readers, and what differs is how much their long-term memory lets each of them put into one slot.

In 1973 William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess players a position for a few seconds and asked them to rebuild it from memory. Masters did far better than novices when the position came from a *real* game. When the same kinds of pieces were set out at random, the masters' advantage largely disappeared.

afterFigure.text: The explanation they offered was chunking. In a real game, pieces stand in familiar patterns, such as a king tucked behind its pawns after castling, and a master holds each pattern as one [[chunk|A single meaningful unit held as one thing, however many items it contains. Met in 'Chunks'.]] where a novice sees separate pieces. **Both are limited to about four chunks**, so what differs is *how much a chunk contains*.

lead.text: Working memory is not a single box. In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that it has several parts. The **central executive** directs attention, deciding what to attend to, what to hold and when to switch, and it stores nothing itself. Beneath it, the **phonological loop** holds speech-based information, and the **visuospatial sketchpad** holds images and positions. In 2000 Baddeley added a fourth part, the **episodic buffer**, which links information from the other parts and from long-term memory into a single coherent episode.
The reason to divide it is that two tasks which use different parts interfere little, while two which use the same part interfere a great deal.
In 1966 Alan Baddeley gave people lists of words to recall in order, some made of words that sound alike and some of words that do not.

Most people lose part of it before the end, because eleven separate digits are more than the mind can hold at once. Now read it as 07700 900 123, the way a phone number is printed, and it becomes much easier, although the digits and their order are exactly the same.

Something has changed between the two versions, and it is not the information. It is the number of things you have to hold, and finding out what counts as a thing explains both the limits of the mind's short-term workspace and how a chess master seems to escape them.

recap.keyIdea: Working memory holds only about four chunks, so what you can hold depends on how much each chunk contains, and that depends on what you already know.

blocks.text: The workspace has a small limit, counted in **chunks** and not in items. *Chunking* uses knowledge in long-term memory to bind several items into one unit, which is how a chess master holds a whole position that a novice sees as scattered pieces. The model of Baddeley and Hitch divides the workspace into a central executive that directs attention, together with stores for sound, for images and space, and for linking.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll follow a memory after it leaves the workspace, and ask how fast it fades and what slows the fading.

lessons.title: Forgetting and spaced retrieval

lead.text: Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables, which have no meaning to help the memory, and found the same shape every time: a steep loss at first, then a loss that grew slower and slower. The plot of how much remains against the time since learning is called the **forgetting curve**.

In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated his procedure with a single volunteer, and their curve had the same shape. It says that an hour of waiting costs *more memory early than late*, and it raises a question that the rest of the lesson answers: can the curve be flattened?

To compare memories we need a number for how long one lasts. Modern scheduling models, including the one behind Discere's reviews, use **stability**, written S: the number of days it takes for the chance of recalling a memory to fall from 100% to 90%. A memory with a stability of 3 days is still recalled 90% of the time after three days, and one with a stability of 12 days takes twelve days to reach that point.

afterFigure.text: Predicted recall after t days is R = 1 ÷ (1 + t ÷ 9S). To check the definition, put t = S in it: the bracket becomes 1 + 1/9, which is 10/9, and R = 9/10, or 90%. A larger S makes the fraction t ÷ 9S grow more slowly, so recall holds up for *longer*, as the second view of the figure shows. This is the form of the curve used in an earlier version of the open-source scheduler that Discere's reviews are based on, and its later versions flatten the tail, so treat the numbers as showing the idea and not as exact predictions of anyone's memory.

lead.text: When you recall something successfully, the act of recalling strengthens the memory, and in the model it multiplies the [[stability|The number of days a memory takes to fall to 90% recall. Met on the previous screen.]] by a growth factor. Suppose a memory with a stability of 2 days is reviewed successfully on day 3, and the review multiplies stability by 2.5. Its stability becomes 5 days, and the curve that follows is flatter than the one it would *otherwise* have had.

afterFigure.text: Reviews spread out over time are **spaced practice**, also called distributed practice, and putting all the study into one sitting is **massed practice**, or cramming. In the scheduler Discere uses, a successful retrieval after more has been forgotten raises stability by more.

Divide the days that have passed by 9S.
Put the ratio into the curve.
So 75% of the memory is predicted to remain, where a stability of 2 days would leave only about 55%.

steps.headline: When the next review is due

lead.text: If [[stability|The number of days a memory takes to fall to 90% recall. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is the number of days to reach 90% recall, it also tells us when to review: the natural moment is when predicted recall has fallen to 90%, which is **S days after the last review**. A memory with S = 2 is due on day 2. A successful review then multiplies S by 2.5 to give 5, so the next review is due 5 days later, on day 7, and the new stability of 12.5 puts the review after that on day 19.5.

afterFigure.text: The gaps between reviews are 2, 5 and 12.5 days, *each longer than the last*, which is why the reviews in the figure spread further apart. A memory you know well comes back rarely and one you struggle with comes back soon, so the effort goes where memory is weakest.

lead.text: A review only counts when it is a retrieval, which means trying to bring the answer to mind and *not just looking at it again*. In 2006 Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students study short prose passages and then either reread a passage or practise recalling it, and a week later those who had practised recall remembered more of the passage's ideas. We call this **retrieval practice**.
Retrieval feels harder and, early on, produces worse scores, so the difference appears only at the delayed test, which is why it is easy to miss.

That pattern is why last night's revision feels solid in the morning and patchy a month later. recap.nextHook: Next we'll look at how behaviour is shaped by what comes before and after it, beginning with conditioning.

lessons.title: Conditioning and reinforcement

lead.text: Pavlov's dogs salivated at food without any training, so he called the food the **unconditioned stimulus** and the salivation it produced the **unconditioned response**. A bell is at first neutral: a dog pricks its ears at it but does not salivate. If the bell sounds just before the food, again and again, the dog begins to salivate at the bell alone, and the bell has become a **conditioned stimulus**, with the salivation it produces a **conditioned response**.

This kind of learning, in which a stimulus comes to trigger a response because it has been paired with another that already does, is **classical conditioning**. What is learned is that one event *predicts* another.

How strongly does the bell predict food after a few pairings? We call the strength of the association **associative strength**, written V. It runs from 0, where the bell predicts nothing, up to a maximum, which we take as 1, where the bell predicts food completely. In 1972 Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner proposed a rule for how V changes on each trial: V goes up by the rate times the gap that remains, so **ΔV = rate × (maximum − V)**. The idea is that a pairing teaches in proportion to how much there is *still to learn*.

afterFigure.text: Take a rate of 0.25 and a start of V = 0. The first pairing adds 0.25 × (1 − 0) = 0.25. The second adds 0.25 × (1 − 0.25) = 0.1875, which makes V = 0.4375, and each pairing after that adds a little less, because the gap that is left keeps shrinking. The figure shows this for two rates: the higher rate climbs faster, but both curves flatten as V approaches the maximum.

lead.text: When the bell keeps sounding and the food stops coming, the same rule applies with one change: with no food the maximum is 0, so V is pulled down by the rate times V, and the dog salivates less and less. This weakening of a learned response when the cue is no longer followed by the outcome is called **extinction**.

afterFigure.text: Extinction is *not* erasure, though. If the dog is rested and the bell sounds again, the salivation often reappears in part, which is called **spontaneous recovery**, and the simple rule cannot explain it, a reminder that the rule is a model and not the whole story.

lead.text: Classical conditioning concerns what comes before a response, and operant conditioning concerns what comes after it. Around 1900 Edward Thorndike found that a cat in a puzzle box, rewarded with escape and food, took less time on each trial to find the way out, and he stated the law of effect: behaviour followed by a satisfying result becomes more likely. B. F. Skinner later studied it in rats and pigeons, in boxes where pressing a lever or pecking a key produced food, and called the learning **operant conditioning** because the animal operates on its environment. A consequence either raises or lowers the behaviour: **reinforcement** makes it more likely, and **punishment** makes it less likely.

A second distinction says whether something is added or taken away. *Positive* means a stimulus is added and *negative* means one is removed, which gives four combinations. A rat given a pellet after pressing a lever presses more, which is positive reinforcement. A person who takes a tablet and finds the headache gone takes tablets more readily, which is negative reinforcement, because something unpleasant was removed and the behaviour rose. A scolding that makes a behaviour rarer is positive punishment, and a fine that takes away money and makes a behaviour rarer is negative punishment. The words do not mean good and bad: negative reinforcement is not a punishment, since the behaviour still rises.

Rewards seldom follow every response, and a schedule of reinforcement says which responses get one. A *ratio* schedule rewards after a number of responses, and an *interval* schedule rewards the first response after a stretch of time has passed. Either can be *fixed*, the same every time, or *variable*, changing around an average. In a **fixed-ratio schedule**, such as FR 4, every fourth response is rewarded. In a **variable-ratio schedule** the reward comes after an unpredictable number of responses that averages, say, four. In a **fixed-interval schedule**, such as FI 10 s, the first response at least 10 seconds after the last reward is rewarded.

afterFigure.text: In their studies published in 1957, Charles Ferster and B. F. Skinner found that a fixed ratio gives bursts of fast responding with a pause after each reward, a variable ratio gives fast, steady responding that is the hardest to extinguish, and a fixed interval gives a pause after each reward and then responding that speeds up as the next one nears.

blocks.text: Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs around the turn of the twentieth century when he noticed that his dogs began to salivate before the food arrived, at the sight of the person who usually fed them. Nothing in a dog's biology makes a person a reason to salivate. The dogs had learned that the person predicts food.

Learning of this kind can be measured, and a rule proposed in 1972 says how much each pairing of a cue with food adds to the association and how quickly it fades once the food stops, so that you can follow it trial by trial. A second kind of learning, in which a behaviour becomes more or less common because of what follows it, explains why rewards that arrive unpredictably keep an animal, or a person at a slot machine, responding long after the rewards have stopped.

recap.keyIdea: Learning follows prediction and consequence: each pairing adds less than the last, a response weakens when its outcome stops, and the schedule of rewards shapes what an animal does.

blocks.text: In classical conditioning a cue gains **associative strength** by the rule ΔV = rate × (maximum − V), so each pairing adds less than the one before, and a cue alone pulls V back towards 0 in extinction. In *operant* conditioning a consequence makes a behaviour more or less likely, and the schedule of rewards, fixed or variable, ratio or interval, shapes the pattern of responding.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll turn from learning to judgement, and see why a positive test result is rarely as conclusive as it feels.

lessons.title: Base rates and Bayes

lead.text: The test's 90% tells you how often the test is positive *among people who have the disease*, but you only know that you tested positive. To answer your question we need to know who all the positives are, and the clearest way to find out is to stop using percentages and count people.

Imagine 1,000 people taking the test. Two in every hundred have the disease, which is 20 people, and the other 980 do not. Counts like these, stated as numbers of people and not as probabilities, are called **natural frequencies**.

The test treats the two groups differently. Among the 20 people who have the disease it detects 90%, which is 18 people, and we call them **true positives** because the test is right about them. Among the 980 who do not have it, the test wrongly flags 5%, which is 49 people, and we call them **false positives**. The share of the population that has the disease before any testing, here 2%, is the **base rate**.

afterFigure.text: So 18 + 49 = 67 people test positive, and only 18 of them have the disease, which is 18 ÷ 67, about 27%. The test is good, and yet a positive result is wrong *nearly three times in four*, because the people without the disease are so much more numerous that even a small false-alarm rate gives them more positives than the sick provide. In the figure the second view is the test we have been counting, and the first is a test that detects only half of the cases: it finds fewer true positives, 10 instead of 18, while the false positives stay at 49.

lead.text: Return to the first guess. Answering '90 in 100' treats the test's hit rate as though it were the chance that a positive result is right, and in doing so it ignores how common the disease is to begin with. Psychologists call this **base-rate neglect**.

It is not only an error of arithmetic. In studies that Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described in 1974, people judged the chance that a man drawn from a group of 30 engineers and 70 lawyers was an engineer by how well a description fitted an engineer, and gave nearly the same answer when the group held 70 engineers and 30 lawyers. Counting the groups, as we did with [[natural frequencies|Counts of people in place of probabilities. Met on the first screen of this lesson.]], puts the base rate in front of you where it is hard to overlook.

The question 'how likely is a person who tested positive to have the disease?' is about the flagged group and nobody else. Everyone in it has tested positive, so the answer is the share of that group who really have the disease: the [[true positives|People who have the condition and test positive. Met earlier in this lesson.]] divided by all the positives, true and false together. That share is called the **positive predictive value**.
Dividing by everyone who has the disease would answer a *different* question, namely how often the test catches the disease, so 18 ÷ (18 + 49) is the only division that matches what was asked.

steps.headline: The share of positives that are true, for 500 people with a base rate of 10%

lead.text: A test has fixed hit and false-alarm rates, but what a positive result means depends on *who* is being tested. Take a test that detects half of the cases and flags 5% of the people without the condition. In a crowd where 2% have the condition, 20 of 1,000 have it, 10 are detected, and 49 of the 980 others are flagged, so 10 of the 59 positives are right, about 17%. In a crowd where 20% have it, 200 have it, 100 are detected, and 40 of the 800 others are flagged, so 100 of the 140 positives are right, about 71%.

afterFigure.text: Nothing about the test changed between the two crowds, **only the [[base rate|The share of the population that has the condition before any testing. Met earlier in this lesson.]]**. That is why a test used to screen everyone can mislead when the same test, used on people who already show symptoms, can be informative, and why a positive result should always be read together with how likely the condition was before the test.

blocks.text: A disease affects 2 people in every 100. A test for it detects 90% of the people who have it, and wrongly flags 5% of the people who don't. You take the test and it comes back positive, and you ask how likely it is that you have the disease.

The answer that comes to mind first is usually close to the 90% that the test is quoted at. Settling it needs no formula, only a careful count of who in a crowd of people tests positive, and the same count tells you how far to trust a positive result from any screening test.

intro.whyItMatters: Medical screening, drug tests and security checks all produce positives, and how far to trust one depends on how common the thing sought is.

blocks.text: Counting people turns a test's hit rate and false-alarm rate into true positives and false positives, and the **positive predictive value** is the true positives divided by all the positives. When a condition is rare, the false positives from the large healthy group can outnumber the true positives, so *ignoring the base rate* leads to confident mistakes.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll look at two more shortcuts of fast thinking, anchoring and availability, and at how to check an intuition with a slower one.

lessons.title: Anchors and fast thinking

lead.text: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiment a wheel of fortune, numbered from 0 to 100, was spun in front of the participants and stopped at a number: for some people it was 10 and for others 65. The participants were then asked whether the percentage of African countries among United Nations members was higher or lower than that number, and after that to give an estimate of their own.

Yet the estimates followed the wheel, and the people who had seen 65 gave larger estimates than those who had seen 10. A number that you meet first and then use as a starting point is an **anchor**, and the habit of adjusting from it *too little* is called **anchoring**. To compare two groups we use the **median**, the middle value when the estimates are put in order, and we measure the gap between two percentages in **percentage points**.

lead.text: If the anchors had no effect, the two medians would be equal, and if the estimates followed the anchors completely, the medians would differ by as much as the anchors do. The **anchoring index** puts the real pull on that scale. It is the difference in [[median|The middle value when estimates are put in order. Met on the first screen of this lesson.]] estimates divided by the difference in anchors, so an index of 0 means the anchors were ignored and an index of 1 means the estimates followed them completely.

afterFigure.text: For the wheel, the medians differed by 20 points and the anchors by 65 − 10 = 55, so the index is 20 ÷ 55, about 0.36: the wheel moved the estimates *about a third as far* as it moved the anchors. Jacowitz and Kahneman proposed the index in 1995, and across a set of general-knowledge questions they found anchors pulling about halfway, an index near 0.5. The second view of the figure shows the arithmetic for made-up guesses, in which anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.

lead.text: Anchoring is one of several **heuristics**, which are quick rules of thumb that the mind uses to judge in a hurry. Another is the **availability heuristic**: we judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, which misleads when ease of recall is caused by something else, such as vividness or recency.

In a study published in 1983 Tversky and Kahneman asked some people how many seven-letter words ending in *ing* they would expect in four pages of a novel, and others how many seven-letter words with n as the sixth letter. Every word ending in *ing* has n as its sixth letter, yet the estimates for *ing* words were nearly three times as high, because the examples we can retrieve easily are not a *fair sample* of the examples that exist.

lead.text: Psychologists often describe fast, automatic, effortless judgement as **System 1** and slow, deliberate, effortful reasoning as **System 2**, and the labels name two *ways of thinking* and not two organs of the brain. System 1 gives us the answer that springs to mind, and System 2 can test it, if we remember to ask.

Shane Frederick built such tests into a short measure of cognitive reflection in 2005. Take a jug and a cup that cost £1.30 together, with the jug costing £1.00 more. The answer that springs to mind is that the cup costs 30p, but the jug would then cost £1.30 and the pair £1.60. Calling the cup's price x, the jug costs x + 100 pence, so 2x + 100 = 130 and the cup costs 15p.
This problem is one of those in Frederick's test, and the figure shows an illustrative group, not his data.

blocks.text: Suppose a wheel numbered from 0 to 100 is spun in front of you and stops at 65. You are then asked whether the percentage of African countries among United Nations members is above or below 65, and what you think it really is. The wheel is plainly random, with nothing to do with Africa or the United Nations, so surely it cannot affect your answer.

Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman ran this experiment and reported it in 1974, in their study of the quick rules of thumb that people use when they have to judge under uncertainty. Its result can be put into a single number, and the same reasoning lets you check how far a price, a first offer or any figure you happen to meet first is steering an estimate of your own, and when a quick answer is worth a slower look.

intro.whyItMatters: Prices, estimates and risk judgements all begin from numbers and examples that happen to be in mind, and knowing how they bias us helps us correct for it.

recap.keyIdea: Fast judgement starts from whatever number or example is in mind, so an estimate should be checked by a slower method.

blocks.text: An **anchor** pulls estimates towards itself, and the anchoring index, the difference in medians divided by the difference in anchors, measures how far. The *availability heuristic* judges frequency by ease of recall, and both are quick rules of thumb that mostly work and fail in predictable ways. A slow check, such as testing a quick answer against the facts of the problem, is the remedy.

recap.nextHook: Next we'll step back from the individual to the group, and read the classic studies of conformity, obedience and bystanders by their numbers.

lessons.title: Conformity, obedience and bystanders

lead.text: In the early 1950s Solomon Asch asked groups of people to say which of three lines matched a standard line, a task on which people working alone almost never got it wrong. But all the members of each group except one were **confederates**, helpers of the experimenter who had been told to give the same wrong answer on certain trials. The one real participant sat near the end of the row and heard the others answer first. Changing your answer to match a group's, as that participant might, is **conformity**.

afterFigure.text: Asch's procedure had 18 trials, and on 12 of them, the **critical trials**, the confederates unanimously gave a wrong answer. The participant's reply on such a trial is a **critical answer**. In the 1956 report of the studies, about 37 in every 100 critical answers went along with the majority, and about 75 in every 100 people went along at least once. The figure shows both numbers, and they count different things, one counting answers and the other counting people.

model.setting: Asch's majority condition, about 37 in every 100 critical answers
Asch's majority condition, about 75 in every 100 people

lead.text: In 1963 Stanley Milgram reported a study of **obedience**, which is acting on the instructions of an authority. Each volunteer was the 'teacher' and had to give a 'learner' a shock for each wrong answer, from a panel of 30 switches labelled from 15 to 450 volts. The learner was really a confederate and received no shocks, and if the teacher hesitated, the experimenter gave a fixed series of prompts, beginning with 'Please continue'.
People asked beforehand predicted that hardly anyone would go on to the end, yet every one of the 40 men reached 300 volts, and most went on to the final switch.

Milgram ran many variations, which he described in his later book, *Obedience to Authority*. In three of them the volunteer's distance from the learner changed. In the first the learner was in another room, and in the second the learner was in the same room as the volunteer. In the third the volunteer had to press the learner's hand down onto a shock plate. The figure shows how many of the 40 volunteers in each version went on to the 450-volt switch, and **obedience fell with each step towards the victim**.

model.setting: Milgram's baseline condition
Milgram's proximity condition
Milgram's touch-proximity condition

lead.text: Asch read his own results *both ways*. Three quarters of his participants conformed at least once, which is striking, yet roughly two thirds of all critical answers were still correct, and a quarter of the people never went along. He also found that a single ally giving the right answer sharply reduced [[conformity|Changing your answer to match a group's. Met earlier in this lesson.]].

Milgram's design could not be repeated in its original form once research ethics changed, but in 2009 Jerry Burger ran a partial replication that stopped at 150 volts. Seventy per cent of Burger's participants continued past the learner's first protest, against 82.5% in the comparable Milgram condition. In 2013 Gina Perry, who read Milgram's papers in the Yale archives, reported that the experimenters did not always keep to the script and that some participants doubted the shocks were real.

Neither the replication nor the archive erases the findings, but together they warn us **not to read the headline percentage as a clean measure of obedience**, and to ask how a result depends on the exact setup.

In 1964 a New York newspaper reported that 38 people had watched the murder of Kitty Genovese and none had called the police, and the story prompted John Darley and Bibb Latané to ask why a person might not help when others are present. Later research, notably by Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins in 2007, found that the story had been *exaggerated*.

In Darley and Latané's experiment, published in 1968, students talked over an intercom from separate booths and heard another student seem to have a seizure. The share who left their booth to report it before the seizure ended fell as the group grew: 85% when alone, 62% with one other, and 31% with four others. Darley and Latané called the effect **diffusion of responsibility**: each person feels less responsible when others could act.

The fall in each person's chance, the [[diffusion of responsibility|Each person feels less responsible when others could act. Met earlier in this lesson.]] you have just met, is not the whole story, because more bystanders also give more chances that somebody acts. If each of n bystanders independently helps with probability p, the chance that nobody helps is (1 − p)ⁿ, so the chance that at least one helps is **1 − (1 − p)ⁿ**. A lone witness who helps with probability 0.85 helps 85% of the time. Three witnesses who each help with probability 0.3 all fail with probability 0.7³ = 0.343, so at least one helps with probability 1 − 0.343 = 0.657, about 66%.

afterFigure.text: In this example the crowd is less likely to produce help than the lone witness, even though there are more people, because each person's chance fell so far. Whether a crowd helps more or less depends on how far each individual's chance falls as the group grows, so the number of bystanders alone settles nothing, and evidence from real events matters.

lead.text: In 2020 Richard Philpot and colleagues analysed CCTV recordings of 219 real public conflicts in three cities. In **91% of them at least one bystander intervened**, and the more bystanders there were, the more likely it was that someone did. A meta-analysis of earlier studies, by Peter Fischer and colleagues in 2011, found a bystander effect on average, with each person less likely to help when others were present, but a much *weaker* one when the emergency was dangerous.
These findings do not cancel the laboratory results, but in real streets, with more people around, it is still more likely that somebody acts.

blocks.text: Asked which of three lines matches a fourth, people working alone almost never make a mistake. Seat the same person at the end of a row of others who, one after another, give the same plainly wrong answer, and in Solomon Asch's studies of the 1950s about three people in every four went along with the group at least once.

Results like this one, and Stanley Milgram's on obedience and John Darley and Bibb Latané's on bystanders, are among the best known in psychology, and they are often retold as proof that the situation simply overrides the person. Reading each one as a rate, set beside the other conditions of the same study and the replications that came later, shows how strong each pull really was and how much it changed with the way the study was run.

intro.whyItMatters: Claims about what crowds, bosses and bystanders make people do often outrun the numbers, and rates let you check them.

recap.keyIdea: The classic studies show real pulls towards the group, authority and the crowd, but their numbers depend on the setup, and later work has qualified each of them.

blocks.text: Conformity, obedience and helping can all be read as **rates**, compared across conditions in percentage points, and the chance that at least one of n bystanders acts is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ. Asch's majority moved many people at least once but not most answers, Milgram's rates fell as the victim came closer, and *replications and archives* have shown that each figure depends on how the study was run. The evidence from real streets is that someone usually steps in.

questions.prompt: Sleep and reaction time correlate at r = −0.6. What percentage of the variation in reaction time do they share?
hints: The shared share of variation comes from squaring r.
A negative number squared is positive.
Square 0.6 and convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Shared variance is r² = (−0.6)² = 0.36, so 36%. Squaring removes the sign.

questions.onCorrect: Squaring r removes the sign: (−0.6)² is 0.36, so a little over a third of the variation is shared.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as if it were already a percentage. The shared share comes from squaring r.
That is the right square, but written as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share left over. The question asks how much is shared.

questions.prompt: Across towns, those with more libraries also have more burglaries, and population size drives both. What do psychologists call a variable like population, which produces a misleading correlation?
hints: It is a hidden third variable that affects both measured variables.
Ask what the two measures share that makes them move together without either pushing the other.

acceptedIdeas: confound
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Population is a confound: a third variable that drives both measures.

questions.onCorrect: A confound drives both measures, so they move together though neither causes the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Reverse causation flips the arrow between two measures. Here a separate variable sits behind both.

questions.prompt: 6 of 20 full-moon shifts were busy, and 30 of 100 other shifts were busy. By how many percentage points does the busy rate differ between the two kinds of shift?
hints: Turn each count into a rate before comparing.
Divide busy shifts by all shifts in each group.
Subtract one rate from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.

questions.onCorrect: The two rates are identical. The full-moon nights were memorable, not more frequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the raw counts, but the two groups differ in size. Turn each count into a rate first.
That compares the quiet shifts, which are different in number. Compare rates, not counts.

questions.prompt: In a drug trial the drug group improves by 12 points and the placebo group by 8 points. How many points of improvement can be attributed to the drug's active ingredient?
hints: The placebo group improves without any active ingredient.
Remove the improvement that both groups share.
Subtract the placebo improvement from the drug improvement.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.

questions.onCorrect: Remove what both groups share. The placebo group shows what expectation and time produce alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drug group's whole improvement, including what expectation alone produces.
That is the improvement without the active ingredient. Ask what the drug added beyond it.
Adding the groups mixes the two responses together. You need what is left after removing the shared part.

questions.prompt: In a trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who measure them know who received the real treatment. What is this design called?
hints: Count how many parties are kept unaware.
Ask whether the people who measure the outcome know which group each person is in.

acceptedIdeas: double-blind
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a double-blind design: both sides are kept unaware of the conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Both sides are kept unaware of the conditions, so neither expectation nor measuring can lean towards the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: A single-blind design keeps only one party unaware. Count how many parties are unaware here.

questions.prompt: A control group scores 100 on average and a training group 106, with a standard deviation of 15 in both. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Cohen's d is a difference measured in standard deviations.
Find the difference between the two means.
Divide that difference by 15.
questions.onCorrect: d is the difference between the means measured in standard deviations, here a gain of 6 beside a spread of 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. Cohen's d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: A replication finds means of 50.4 (depleted) and 50.0 (control), both with standard deviation 10. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Divide the difference between means by the standard deviation.
The difference between the means is under one point.
Divide 0.4 by 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: The means differ by well under a tenth of a standard deviation, so the published effect did not appear.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference in points. Divide it by the standard deviation.
That divides the SD by the difference. d divides the difference by the SD.

hints: Divide the successful replications by the studies attempted.
Use 97 as the denominator, since only significant originals count.
Convert 35/97 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Only the 97 originals with significant results count, and 35 of their replications held up, a little over a third.

That is the share that did not replicate. The question asks for the share that did.

questions.prompt: Lowering the criterion so an observer says yes more often increases hits. Which other outcome, on trials with no signal, does it also increase?
hints: Think about the yes responses on trials with no signal.
Think about what happens on the quiet nights when the guard shouts more readily.

acceptedIdeas: false alarms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It also increases false alarms: more yes responses when no signal is present.

questions.onCorrect: A lower criterion means more yes answers everywhere, including on trials where there is only noise.

More yes answers means fewer correct rejections, not more.

questions.prompt: An observer concentrating on a task fails to see a clearly visible but unexpected object. What is this failure called?
hints: It is a kind of blindness caused by where attention was directed.
The object was in plain view, so what was missing was attention and not eyesight.

acceptedIdeas: inattentional blindness
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.

questions.onCorrect: The object was visible but not attended, so it went unseen. That is inattentional blindness.

misconceptions.feedback: Change blindness is missing a change between two views. Here the object was never attended.

questions.prompt: Vision reads 50 mm with an SD of 2 mm, and touch reads 56 mm with an SD of 4 mm. What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Reliability is one over the variance, 1/SD².
Vision's share is its reliability divided by the sum of both.
Multiply each reading by its share and add.

questions.onCorrect: The weights follow 1 ÷ SD², so the steadier cue counts for four times as much as the other and the estimate lies well away from the midpoint.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to touch, but touch is the less reliable cue here.

questions.prompt: Perception guided by knowledge and expectation, rather than built only from incoming sensory features, is called what kind of processing?
hints: It runs in the opposite direction to bottom-up processing.
Bottom-up processing starts from the incoming features. Which direction does knowledge push from?

acceptedIdeas: top-down
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Top-down processing: knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived. That is top-down, the reverse of building from features.

misconceptions.feedback: Bottom-up builds perception from the incoming features alone. This asks for the opposite direction.

acceptedIdeas: Phonological loop

Visuospatial sketchpad

Phonological loop

questions.prompt: What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called?
hints: The groups are called chunks.
