questions.onCorrect: Spreading study over days is distributed, or spaced, practice, the opposite of cramming.

The wins arrive after an unpredictable number of plays and not after a fixed wait.

Negative means taken away, and punishment means the behaviour becomes less common.

Negative punishment
Negative reinforcement

questions.prompt: In a screening of 1,000 people, 1% have a disease. The test detects 90% of the people who have it and wrongly flags 10% of the people who don't. A person tests positive. What is the probability, as a percentage, that they have the disease? Give one decimal place.

The true positives are the people in that group who have the disease.
Divide 9 by the total number of positives and round.
questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives, and not the test's hit rate: most of the positives here are false alarms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate. The question asks how many positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.
That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.

questions.prompt: 20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place.
hints: Imagine 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.
The witness calls 75% of blue cabs blue and 25% of green cabs blue.
Divide correct 'blue' calls by all 'blue' calls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

questions.onCorrect: Count the cabs the witness calls blue: the true calls over all the calls. The many green cabs produce many wrong ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the witness's accuracy, not the chance that this cab was blue.
That is the base rate alone. The witness's report adds evidence.
That is the share of 'blue' calls that were wrong.

questions.prompt: A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called?
hints: The neglected number is how common the condition is to begin with.
The doctor treats the test's hit rate as the chance that a positive is right. What did the doctor leave out?

acceptedIdeas: base-rate neglect
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

questions.onCorrect: Ignoring how rare a condition is when judging a result is base-rate neglect.

misconceptions.feedback: Confirmation bias favours evidence that fits what you believe. This error ignores how common the condition is.

questions.prompt: Anchors of 20 and 80 years produce median estimates of 35 and 59 years for the age of an oak tree. What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)?
hints: Find the gap between the median estimates.
Find the gap between the anchors.
Divide the first gap by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The estimates moved 24 years for an anchor gap of 60, a clear pull but not a full one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in medians alone. Divide it by the gap between the anchors.
That divides the gap between anchors by the gap in medians. Invert it.

questions.prompt: After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic?
hints: The examples are readily available in memory.
It is a rule of thumb that treats cases that are easy to recall as cases that are common.

acceptedIdeas: availability
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.

questions.onCorrect: Vivid, easily recalled cases feel common. That is the availability heuristic.

misconceptions.feedback: Anchoring is the pull of a starting number. This is about how easily examples come to mind.

questions.prompt: In the first version 26 of 40 volunteers obeyed to the end, and with the volunteer's hand pressing the learner's onto the plate 12 of 40 did. By how many percentage points did obedience fall?
hints: Turn each count into a percentage.
Both conditions had 40 participants.
Subtract the touch-proximity percentage from the baseline percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Turn each count into a percentage and subtract: closeness to the victim cut obedience sharply.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the baseline rate alone. Subtract the touch-proximity rate from it.
That is the touch-proximity rate alone. Find the gap between the two rates.
That is a difference in people. The question asks for percentage points.

questions.prompt: People in Tversky and Kahneman's experiment saw a wheel stop at 10 or at 65 and then estimated the percentage of African countries among United Nations members. The wheel was plainly random. What made the result striking?
hints: Would you expect a spinning wheel to tell you anything about the United Nations?
Compare the estimates of the two groups.

acceptedIdeas: The estimates followed the random number, with higher guesses after 65
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The estimates followed the random number, with higher guesses after 65

choices.label: The wheel gave people useful information about the answer they were asked for
People ignored the wheel and answered from what they knew about Africa
The estimates followed the random number, with higher guesses after 65

questions.onCorrect: A number everyone could see was random still pulled the estimates towards it. The medians differed by 20 points when the anchors differed by 55.

misconceptions.feedback: The wheel was plainly random and had nothing to do with Africa or the United Nations. That is why the pull it had was striking.
The estimates followed the wheel: those who saw 65 gave larger estimates than those who saw 10.

questions.prompt: What does an anchoring index of 0.35 say?
hints: Think about what an index of 0 means, and what an index of 1 means.
An index of 0.35 sits between those two values, nearer the first than the second.

acceptedIdeas: The medians moved about a third as far as the anchors did
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An index between 0 and 1 shows how far the estimates moved, as a share of the anchors' gap.

choices.label: The medians moved about a third as far as the anchors did
The medians moved exactly as far as the anchors did, no more and no less
The estimates ignored the anchors completely and stayed where they were

questions.onCorrect: An index of 0.35 means that about a third of the anchors' gap showed up in the estimates.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be an index of 0.
That would be an index of 1.

questions.prompt: In the sequence AABAB, why are there 3 switches in 5 trials?
hints: Look at each pair of neighbouring trials. Is the task different?
The first trial has nothing before it, so start comparing from the second.

acceptedIdeas: Only changes count, and the first two trials match
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only changes count, and the first two trials match

choices.label: Only changes count, and the first two trials match
Every trial after the first counts as a switch in the sequence
Every second trial in the sequence is a switch

questions.onCorrect: Only a change of task is a switch, and two As in a row are not.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make four switches, not three. Check each trial against the one before it.
Switches depend on which task follows which, not on a fixed spacing.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease?
hints: Who is the question about: everyone, or someone who tested positive?
A person who has tested positive belongs to the group of positives and to no other group.

acceptedIdeas: The question is about people who tested positive, and 120 did
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question is about people who tested positive, and 120 did

choices.label: The question is about people who tested positive, and 120 did
The 50 people who have the disease should not be counted at all
A percentage is always taken out of the larger of the two numbers

questions.onCorrect: The person has tested positive, so they are one of the flagged, and that group is what we divide by.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of a number does not decide the denominator. The question being asked does.
The 50 do count: the ones among them who tested positive are the true positives.

questions.prompt: Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial?
hints: What does the bell now predict?
With no food, the value the bell moves towards is 0. Is V above or below it?

acceptedIdeas: The maximum is now 0, which is below V
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The maximum is now 0, which is below V

choices.label: The maximum is now 0, which is below V
The bell wears out the more it is used
The dog forgets the bell as time passes

questions.onCorrect: With no food the maximum is 0, so the gap is negative and V moves down.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule has no wear-out term. The change comes from the gap between V and the maximum.
Time does not appear in the rule. The change comes from the gap between V and the maximum.

questions.prompt: Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Which consequence is this?
hints: Was something added or removed, and did the behaviour rise or fall?
Positive means something is added and negative means something is removed.

acceptedIdeas: Positive reinforcement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.

choices.label: Positive reinforcement
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement

questions.onCorrect: Something was added and the behaviour rose, so it is positive reinforcement.

misconceptions.feedback: Negative means something is removed. Nothing was taken away here: praise was added.
Punishment makes the behaviour less likely, and here the hand-raising became more frequent.

questions.prompt: Ice-cream takings and pool rescues in a seaside town rise and fall together through the summer. What best explains why?
hints: Ask what else changes across the year.
Takings and rescues are both highest in the same weeks. What do those weeks have in common?

acceptedIdeas: Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.

choices.label: Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
Eating ice cream makes swimmers cramp, so they are more likely to need rescuing.
Rescues make onlookers want to go and buy ice cream.

questions.onCorrect: Something outside both lists can move them together, and the weather is the obvious candidate. We'll give that idea a name once we've seen how to measure a pattern like this.

misconceptions.feedback: That could be so in principle, but nothing in the pattern shows it. Ask instead what else changes through the summer that could affect both lists.
The pattern doesn't point that way either. Look for something that changes across the summer and could affect both lists at once.

questions.prompt: Is a correlation of r = −0.6 stronger or weaker than one of r = +0.4?
hints: Strength is how far r lies from 0.
Ignore the signs when you compare the sizes.

acceptedIdeas: Stronger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stronger

choices.label: Stronger
They can't be compared, because one is negative
Weaker

questions.onCorrect: Strength is the distance from 0, so −0.6 is stronger than +0.4. The sign gives only the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: A plus sign shows the direction of a pattern, not its strength. Set both signs aside and compare 0.6 with 0.4.
A minus sign only says that one measure falls as the other rises. Both numbers can still be compared by how far each lies from 0.

questions.prompt: Children with bigger shoe sizes tend to read better. Which is the most likely confound?
hints: A confound is a third factor that drives both measures.
What changes both a child's shoe size and how well they read?

acceptedIdeas: The children's ages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Age: older children have bigger feet and have also had longer to learn to read.

choices.label: How many books they own
Their foot size
The children's ages

questions.onCorrect: Age moves both measures together: older children have bigger feet and have had more years of reading practice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two measures, not a third factor behind them. A confound sits outside both lists.
Books at home might help reading, but they give feet no reason to grow. A confound has to plausibly move both measures.

questions.prompt: A course lifts scores by 6 points in two classes. Scores in class A usually differ from the class average by about 3 points, and in class B by about 30. In which class is the 6-point gain more impressive?
hints: Think about how easily a 6-point gain could be noise.
In which class would a 6-point change stand out from the usual variation?

acceptedIdeas: Class A, where scores vary little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Class A: against a spread of about 3 points, a 6-point gain is large.

choices.label: Class B, where scores vary a lot
Neither, because the gain is the same size in both classes
Class A, where scores vary little

questions.onCorrect: A gain is judged against the ordinary scatter of scores. Beside a scatter of 3 points, a gain of 6 stands out, and beside 30 it is lost.

misconceptions.feedback: With a spread of about 30, a 6-point gain is lost in the ordinary variation.
The same raw gain means different things beside different spreads.

questions.prompt: Why not simply average the two standard deviations?
hints: Which of the two groups has more spread, and which number should count for more?
Squaring before averaging lets the larger SD have more say.

acceptedIdeas: The more spread-out group should carry more weight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The more spread-out group should carry more weight

choices.label: Standard deviations cannot be averaged at all
The more spread-out group should carry more weight
Squaring is needed only to make the numbers positive

questions.onCorrect: Working from the squares lets the more spread-out group count for more, as it does in the data.

misconceptions.feedback: Averaging is allowed in arithmetic. The pooled value is simply a better combination when the spreads differ.
Standard deviations are already positive, so the squaring serves another purpose.

questions.prompt: Twenty small studies, each with 15 people per group, test the same small effect, which is real. What pattern of results is most likely?
hints: Think about the power of each study, and about which estimates come out significant.
A small study can reach significance only when its estimate overshoots.

acceptedIdeas: Most are non-significant, and the few that are significant overestimate the effect
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most are non-significant, and the few that are significant overestimate the effect

choices.label: None is significant, because the effect is too small to detect
About as many are significant as in twenty large studies, with accurate estimates
Most are non-significant, and the few that are significant underestimate the effect
Most are non-significant, and the few that are significant overestimate the effect

questions.onCorrect: If only the significant studies were published, the literature would show an effect larger than the real one, which is one reason replications often find smaller effects.

misconceptions.feedback: Low power makes a significant result uncommon, not impossible, and with twenty tries a few are likely to reach it.
Power depends on the number of people, and with 15 per group each study has much less of it than a large one.
Consider which small studies cross the significance line: the ones whose estimate happened to come out high. Which way does that push the estimates that get reported?

questions.prompt: Researchers draw the names of 20 volunteers at random, and the treatment group turns out to average two years older than the control group. Why is that gap no problem for random assignment?
hints: Does one draw guarantee equal groups, or only fairness?
What is a random draw guaranteed to do, and what is it not guaranteed to do?

acceptedIdeas: Because chance leaves small gaps, and either group could be older
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because chance leaves small gaps, and either group could be older

choices.label: Because the treatment will cancel out the age difference between them
Because random assignment makes the two groups exactly identical in age
Because chance leaves small gaps, and either group could be older

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment promises only that no trait leans systematically one way, so a two-year gap in a small study is an ordinary result of chance.

misconceptions.feedback: One draw of 20 people cannot make two groups identical, and the two-year gap is the proof.
The treatment cannot change anyone's age, and the gap exists before it is given. The question is why the gap is not a flaw in the design.

questions.prompt: Why give the control group an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient?
hints: What else, besides the drug, might make people improve?
If both groups expect to improve, what difference is left between them?

acceptedIdeas: So that expectation is the same in both groups
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps expectation equal, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.

choices.label: So that expectation is the same in both groups
So that the control group cannot improve
So that the drug group takes longer to improve

questions.onCorrect: Equal-looking pills mean equal expectation, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.

misconceptions.feedback: The control group can still improve through expectation and time, and the pill is there so that we can see how much.
The pill is about what people expect, not how long anything takes.

questions.prompt: Why does a larger stability slow forgetting?
hints: Look at which number sits under the fraction.
S sits inside 9S. What happens to t ÷ 9S as S grows?

acceptedIdeas: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly

choices.label: It makes t smaller, so fewer days have passed since learning
It makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows more slowly
It adds a fixed amount to the recall each day

questions.onCorrect: S sits under the fraction, so a bigger S makes the ratio grow more slowly and recall holds up for longer.

misconceptions.feedback: The days that have passed are the same whatever the stability is. Only the ratio changes.
Recall is never added to. It falls as the ratio grows.

questions.prompt: Your eyes judge the block's height as 50 mm, and your gloved fingers judge it as 56 mm. Your eyes, in good light, are the steadier of the two. Roughly where should your best single estimate of the height land?
hints: Which of the two senses would you trust more here?
Should a trusted cue count for the same as a doubtful one?

acceptedIdeas: Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closer to 50 mm: your eyes are the more reliable cue, so they should count for more.

choices.label: Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm
Closer to 56 mm than to 50 mm
Exactly halfway, at 53 mm

questions.onCorrect: A steadier cue should count for more, and you leaned towards sight before anyone gave you a rule.

misconceptions.feedback: The midpoint treats both cues as equally trustworthy, and the question says that they are not.
That follows the gloved fingers, which are the less steady cue.

questions.prompt: Why does the answer land nearer 30 than the midpoint, 33?
hints: Which cue has the smaller SD?
Compare the weights of the two cues, 1 ÷ SD² for each.

acceptedIdeas: The steadier cue's reading, 30, carries more weight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steadier cue's reading, 30, carries more weight

choices.label: The first reading listed always counts for more than the second
The smaller reading always counts for more
The steadier cue's reading, 30, carries more weight

questions.onCorrect: The estimate leans towards the steadier cue's reading, which is the one with the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: Order does not matter. Only the SDs set the weights.
The size of a reading does not matter. Only reliability sets the weight.

questions.prompt: Two independent cues have SDs of 4 mm and 6 mm. How does the SD of the combined estimate compare with them?
hints: Their reliabilities add, so does the total reliability go up or down?
A larger total reliability means a smaller combined SD.

acceptedIdeas: It is smaller than 4 mm, because the reliabilities add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is smaller than 4 mm, because the reliabilities add

choices.label: It lies between 4 mm and 6 mm, as an average of the two would
It stays at 4 mm, since the weaker cue adds nothing to the steadier one
It is smaller than 4 mm, because the reliabilities add

questions.onCorrect: The combined reliability is 1/16 + 1/36, so the combined SD is about 3.3 mm. Every independent cue adds information, which is why the estimate ends up below the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: An average would land there, but reliabilities add. The combined estimate is steadier than the better cue, which is why combining pays.
Even a weaker independent cue helps a little: 1/16 + 1/36 gives a combined SD of about 3.3 mm.

questions.prompt: A thief came on 10 of 20 nights. Guard A shouted on all 10 thief nights and on 9 of the 10 quiet nights. Guard B shouted on 8 of the thief nights and on 1 of the quiet nights. Which guard is better at telling a thief night from a quiet night?
hints: Look at what each guard does on the quiet nights as well.
Does shouting on every night show that a guard can tell the nights apart?

acceptedIdeas: Guard B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guard B: he shouts far more often on thief nights than on quiet nights. Guard A shouts almost whatever happens.

choices.label: Neither, because they are equally good
Guard A
Guard B

questions.onCorrect: Telling the nights apart means shouting far more often on thief nights than on quiet ones. Guard B's two rates are far apart, and Guard A's are almost the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Guard A shouts on almost every night, thief or not. That shows how willing A is to shout, not how well A can tell the nights apart.
The two guards shout at very different rates on the two kinds of night. Compare each guard's pair of rates.

questions.prompt: A smoke alarm stays silent while a fire is burning in the room. In signal-detection terms, what is that outcome called?
hints: Was there a signal, and did the alarm respond to it?
Silence when a signal is present has a name among the four outcomes.

acceptedIdeas: miss
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The signal, a fire, was present and the alarm gave no response: a miss.

questions.onCorrect: A fire was there and the alarm stayed silent, which is a miss, the costlier of the two mistakes for a smoke alarm.

misconceptions.feedback: A false alarm is a response when there is no signal, such as the alarm sounding at burnt toast.
A hit is a response when the signal is there, such as the alarm sounding during a fire.
A correct rejection is silence when there is no signal, such as a quiet alarm in an empty kitchen.

questions.prompt: Why does subtracting z(FA) make d′ larger here?
hints: What is subtracting a negative number the same as?
Try the sum with the two z-scores from the worked line.

acceptedIdeas: z(FA) is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: z(FA) is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size

choices.label: z(FA) is below zero, so subtracting it adds its size
The minus sign in the formula flips every number it meets
d′ must always come out larger than either z-score

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting a negative number adds its size, so a low false-alarm rate raises d′.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the number after the minus sign changes sign. The first z-score keeps its own.
d′ is a difference, so it can be smaller than a z-score, as it would be if both z-scores were close together.

questions.prompt: After a tumour she missed leads to a complaint, a radiologist begins reporting more scans as suspicious. In signal-detection terms, what has most likely changed?
hints: Has she become better at seeing tumours, or more ready to say a scan might show one?
A complaint about a miss changes what a miss costs. Does it change how well she sees?

acceptedIdeas: The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Costs and rewards move the criterion. The curves have not moved, so sensitivity is the same.

choices.label: Sensitivity has fallen, because the observer is less careful
Sensitivity and criterion have both changed, since they measure one thing
The criterion has moved, while sensitivity can stay the same

questions.onCorrect: Costs and rewards move the criterion line. The curves stay put, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Saying yes more readily is not carelessness. The line has moved, and the curves have not.
They are separate measures, and one can change while the other stays put.

questions.prompt: You are repeating a phone number under your breath when someone asks you a question, and you stop rehearsing to answer them. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's model decided to move your attention?
hints: Which part is a controller rather than a store?
The part that decides is not a store of sounds or of images.

acceptedIdeas: central executive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive, which decides what to attend to and when to switch, moved attention from the number to the question.

questions.onCorrect: The central executive made the switch, while the number itself was being held in the phonological loop.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad stores images and positions. It does not direct attention.
The buffer links stored material. Directing attention is another job.
The phonological loop was holding the number. Deciding to stop and attend to the question is the controller's job.

questions.prompt: A gym finds that members who took its fitness programme ended up fitter than members who didn't. Does that show the programme works?
hints: Ask who chose to take the programme.
Would the people who signed up have been the same as the people who didn't, before it began?

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily, because the members who joined may have been fitter already
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily, because the members who joined may have been fitter already

choices.label: Not necessarily, because the members who joined may have been fitter already
Yes, because the members who took the programme ended up fitter than the rest
No, because a gym has no reliable way to measure fitness

questions.onCorrect: People who choose a programme can differ from those who don't before it starts, and the gym's records can't show how much of the gap that explains.

misconceptions.feedback: Ending up fitter is what we would see if the programme worked, but also if the keenest and fittest members were the ones who signed up. The result alone can't separate the two.
Fitness can be measured, by a timed run or a heart rate for instance. The difficulty lies in how the two groups came to exist, not in the measuring.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 2 people in every 100. A test detects 90% of the people who have it and wrongly flags 5% of the people who don't. A person tests positive. Roughly how likely is it that they have the disease?
hints: Imagine 1,000 people taking the test and count who ends up with a positive result.
How many of the people who test positive actually have the disease?

acceptedIdeas: About 27 in 100
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 27 in 100: of 67 positives among 1,000 people, 18 have the disease.

choices.label: About 90 in 100
About 27 in 100
About 50 in 100

questions.onCorrect: Counting 1,000 people gives 18 who have the disease and test positive among 67 positives in all, a little over a quarter. We'll build that count step by step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate, which answers a different question: how often the test is positive among people who have the disease, not how often people who test positive have it.
That would be right only if as many people had the disease as did not, and here far fewer do.

questions.prompt: One group of people saw the wheel stop at 10, and another group saw it stop at 65. Which group gave the higher estimates, typically, of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations?
hints: Think about which direction a number you have just seen would pull your own estimate.
An anchor pulls estimates towards itself.

acceptedIdeas: The group that saw 65
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The group that saw 65 gave the higher estimates.

choices.label: The group that saw 10
Neither: the two groups gave the same estimates
The group that saw 65

questions.onCorrect: The group that saw 65 guessed higher, though the wheel was plainly random. The next screens give the numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: The wheel was random, and the pull of a number goes towards that number, so the lower number would pull estimates down and not up.
If a random number could not touch the answer, the two groups would match. They did not, and the gap is what we will measure.

questions.prompt: In a 2013 study, 20 of 24 radiologists searching lung scans for small nodules failed to notice a picture of a gorilla, 48 times the size of a typical nodule, placed in the last scan. Eye-tracking showed that most of those who missed it had looked straight at it. What best explains this?
hints: Ask where the radiologists' attention was while their eyes passed over the gorilla.
The eye-tracking showed the radiologists' eyes passing over it. What does that say about looking and seeing?

acceptedIdeas: Their attention was on the nodules, so the unexpected gorilla did not register
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their attention was on the nodules, so the unexpected gorilla did not register

choices.label: The gorilla was too small and too faint to be seen clearly on the scans
Their attention was on the nodules, so the unexpected gorilla did not register
The radiologists saw the gorilla but forgot it before they were asked about it

questions.onCorrect: This is inattentional blindness in experts: years of practice at reading scans did not protect them, because looking at something does not guarantee seeing it.

misconceptions.feedback: The gorilla was 48 times the size of a typical nodule, the very thing they were searching for, and most of those who missed it looked straight at it, so its size cannot explain the miss.
Forgetting would not explain why so many experts failed to notice it while their eyes rested on it. What held their attention was the search for nodules, so the gorilla never registered.

questions.prompt: In Watson and Strayer's study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. A friend says they drive just as well while on a demanding phone call. What does the study suggest about the claim?
hints: Work out what share of the 200 drivers showed no cost.
What does 5 in 200 say about what to expect from any single driver?

acceptedIdeas: It is probably wrong, because only about 1 driver in 40 showed no cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only 5 of 200 drivers, 2.5%, showed no cost, so for any one driver a cost is far likelier.

choices.label: It is probably wrong, because only about 1 driver in 40 showed no cost
It is probably right, because the study found drivers who showed no cost
The study says nothing about it, because it used a simulator

questions.onCorrect: Supertaskers exist, which matters for the science, but at 2.5% of drivers the sensible expectation for any one person is a cost.

misconceptions.feedback: The study did find such drivers, but only 5 of 200, or 2.5%, so for any one driver the likelier case by far is a cost.
A simulator is not a road, but it let Watson and Strayer compare each driver alone and under a double load, and the great majority did worse when the two were combined.

questions.prompt: Nine digits with no pattern are read out one at a time, and working memory holds about four chunks. What happens when you try to hold all nine?
hints: Ask how many chunks nine separate digits make.
Compare nine chunks with the limit of about four.

acceptedIdeas: Only about four fit, because each patternless digit takes a chunk of its own
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nine separate digits are nine chunks, so only about four can be held and the rest are lost.

choices.label: Only about four fit, because each patternless digit takes a chunk of its own
All nine fit, because each digit is a small item
All nine fit as three chunks of three, because the mind groups digits by itself

questions.onCorrect: With no pattern to bind them, five of the nine digits have no slot, which is why a long string of random digits slips away.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit counts chunks, however small each item is, and nine separate digits are nine chunks, more than twice what the workspace holds.
Grouping helps only when the groups are something you already know, such as the shape of a phone number, and digits with no pattern give you nothing to group them by.

questions.prompt: A student has a test in a week and a second evening to spend on a chapter she has already read once. Which use of that evening is likely to leave her remembering more of the chapter at the test?
hints: Think about which kind of review did better at the delayed test in Roediger and Karpicke's study.
The advantage of retrieval shows at the delayed test and not straight away.

acceptedIdeas: Closing the book, writing down what she can recall, and then checking it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Practising recall, because retrieval strengthens the memory and its advantage shows at a delayed test.

choices.label: Closing the book, writing down what she can recall, and then checking it
Either, since both spend the same time on the chapter
Reading the chapter through again, since it will feel more familiar to her

questions.onCorrect: Recall is harder work and may feel less satisfying on the night, but it is the kind of review that is still paying off a week later.

misconceptions.feedback: Rereading makes the chapter feel familiar, but in Roediger and Karpicke's study that fluency did not last, and at the test a week later the students who had practised recall remembered more.
The time is the same, yet trying to bring the ideas to mind strengthens the memory more than looking at them again, which is why recall did better at the delayed test.

questions.prompt: On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, the first press at least 10 seconds after the previous reward is rewarded. A rat presses the lever every 3 seconds. How often does it earn a reward?
hints: List the times of the presses, 3, 6, 9, 12 and so on, and find the first one at or after 10 seconds.
Only the first press after the 10 seconds counts, and the clock restarts at each reward.

acceptedIdeas: Every 12 seconds, at the first press after 10 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every 12 seconds, at the first press after 10 seconds

choices.label: Every 12 seconds, at the first press after 10 seconds
Every 10 seconds, as soon as each interval ends
Every 3 seconds, at each press after the first 10 seconds

questions.onCorrect: Rewards come at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 seconds, five in a minute, because the rat's presses never land exactly on the 10-second mark.

misconceptions.feedback: The interval only makes a reward available, and a press still has to collect it. List the rat's press times and see when the first one after the interval comes.
Once a reward is collected the clock starts again, so presses in the next 10 seconds earn nothing, and only the first press after that is rewarded.

questions.prompt: In an illustrative sample of 600 words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter, yet most people judge that more words start with k. Why?
hints: Try to think of words that start with k, and then of words with k as the third letter.
Which is easier to retrieve: words by how they begin, or words by a letter buried in the middle?

acceptedIdeas: Memory is searched by first letter, so words starting with k come to mind more easily
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Words that start with k are easy to retrieve because memory is searched by first letter, so they seem more common than they are.

choices.label: People have met more words that start with k than words with k as the third letter
Memory is searched by first letter, so words starting with k come to mind more easily
People answer almost at random, because they cannot judge how common a letter is

questions.onCorrect: Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind is the availability heuristic, and here ease of recall reflects how memory is searched, not how often the words occur.

misconceptions.feedback: In this sample, words with k as the third letter outnumber those that start with it two to one, so people's reading runs the other way. What differs is how easily each kind comes to mind.
Random guesses would scatter both ways, while people's answers lean the same way, towards the first letter, which points to a systematic cause.

questions.prompt: In Asch's 1956 report, about 37 in every 100 critical answers went along with the wrong majority, while about 75 in every 100 people went along at least once. How can both figures be true?
hints: Ask what each figure counts: answers, or people.
A person who conforms on just one of the twelve trials counts once as a person and once as an answer.

acceptedIdeas: Many people conformed on only some of their 12 critical trials
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many people conformed on only some of their 12 critical trials

choices.label: Many people conformed on only some of their 12 critical trials
Some people gave more than 12 critical answers each
They come from different experiments, so they cannot both describe one study

questions.onCorrect: Asch read his results both ways for this reason: three quarters of the people conformed at least once, yet roughly two thirds of all critical answers were still correct.

misconceptions.feedback: Both come from the same studies. One counts answers and the other counts people, which is why they differ.
Every participant faced the same 12 critical trials. The figures differ because one is a share of answers and the other a share of people.

questions.prompt: Across a sample of students, weekly hours of study and exam grades correlate at r = 0.4. Which explanation has the arrow running from grades to studying?
hints: Reverse causation flips which measure is the cause.
The arrow starts at the cause. Which option has grades as the cause and studying as the result?

acceptedIdeas: Students who are doing well are encouraged to study more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Students who are doing well are encouraged to study more

choices.label: Studying more hours raises students' grades
Highly motivated students both study more and score higher
Students who are doing well are encouraged to study more

questions.onCorrect: When the arrow runs from grades to studying, doing well leads to more studying. The correlation alone cannot rule that out.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the arrow running from studying to grades, which is the direction the numbers seem to suggest.
That puts a third factor behind both measures, so no arrow runs between studying and grades at all.

questions.prompt: Some researchers publish their hypothesis, sample size and analysis plan before they collect any data, which limits their room for flexible analysis choices. What is this practice called?
hints: Think about what the researchers do before they collect any data.
The plan is made public, so that later choices can be checked against it.

acceptedIdeas: preregistration
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: preregistration

questions.onCorrect: Publishing the plan first leaves less room to choose an analysis after seeing the data.

misconceptions.feedback: A replication repeats a study with new participants. This asks about a plan that is published before any data exist.
Power is the chance that a study finds an effect that is real. This asks about publishing the plan beforehand.

questions.prompt: Six explanations have been offered for correlations, and the cases are invented. Which kind of explanation is each one?
hints: For each case, ask whether a third factor, the opposite arrow or a trick of memory is doing the work.
A confound moves both measures. Reverse causation makes the second measure the cause of the first.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ice-cream and vocabulary cases are confounds, since weather and age move both measures. The television and hospital cases are reverse causation. The lucky shirt and the rainy days are illusory correlations kept alive by memory.

items.label: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together because both depend on hot weather
items.explanation: The weather is a third factor that drives both measures.

items.label: People who watch more television report lower moods, and the researchers suggest that low mood sends people to the sofa
items.explanation: The arrow is flipped: mood is proposed as the cause of viewing.

items.label: A coach remembers the matches won in his lucky shirt and forgets the ones lost in it
items.explanation: Memory keeps the cases that stood out, and a full count would show no link.

items.label: Children's vocabulary and shoe size rise together because both grow with age
items.explanation: Age drives both measures, so they move together with no push between them.

items.label: Patients who spend longer in hospital have worse health later, and the sickest patients are the ones kept in
items.explanation: Poor health is the cause of the long stay, not its result.

items.label: A teacher is sure that rowdy classes follow rainy days, but a count shows the same share on dry days
items.explanation: The rainy afternoons are vivid, and the counted rates show no difference.

questions.onCorrect: One correlation can arise in three ways, so the number alone never says which. Each case needs its own check: hold the third factor still, look for the opposite arrow, or compare the full counts.

questions.prompt: A survey of 800 students finds that those who use a study app score higher in exams, with r = 0.35, and the company says the app raises scores. Which new evidence would do the most to support that claim?
hints: Ask what would stop keen students from being the ones who use the app.
Which design lets the researchers decide who gets the app?

acceptedIdeas: A comparison in which a lottery decides which students get the app
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comparison in which a lottery decides which students get the app

choices.label: A survey of 8,000 students that finds the same correlation of r = 0.35
A survey that finds a stronger correlation, such as r = 0.6, in the same group
A comparison in which a lottery decides which students get the app

questions.onCorrect: When a lottery decides who gets the app, motivation cannot be what separates the groups, which a larger or tighter survey cannot promise. The next lesson explains why.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger sample makes r more precise, but keen students could still be the ones using the app, so it cannot show a cause.
A stronger correlation is still an association. Motivated students may use the app and study more, however large r is.

questions.prompt: Four gym members who chose a fitness programme exercised 8 hours a week on average before it began, and four who chose not to exercised 2 hours. Three months later the programme group is fitter. Why is that a poor reason to say the programme works?
hints: Compare the two groups before the programme starts.
Who decided which group each member joined?

acceptedIdeas: The groups already differed in how much they exercised before it began
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The groups already differed in how much they exercised before it began

choices.label: The groups already differed in how much they exercised before it began
Eight people is too few for any comparison to mean anything at all
Fitness gains can only be judged properly after a full year or more

questions.onCorrect: The members chose their own group, so the keener, fitter ones were already in the programme group. The gap at the end mixes the programme's effect with that head start, which is self-selection.

misconceptions.feedback: Small groups give rough averages, but the sharper problem is the six-hour gap that existed before anyone took part.
Three months is long enough to measure a change in fitness. The trouble is that the two groups were not alike at the start.

questions.prompt: Researchers draw names at random to give 60 students either 6 or 9 hours of sleep a night for a week, and then test how many words each student recalls. The study is invented. What part does each of these play?
hints: The researchers set one of these and only measure another.
A trait a student brings with them was not set by the researchers.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hours of sleep given is the independent variable. The words recalled and the later test score are dependent variables. Prior memory and usual sleep are traits that random assignment spreads between the groups.

bins.label: Trait that random assignment spreads between the groups

items.label: Whether a student is given 6 or 9 hours of sleep
items.explanation: The researchers set it, and it is what the two groups differ in on purpose.

items.label: The number of words recalled the next morning
items.explanation: It is measured to see the effect of the sleep that was set.

items.label: How good each student's memory was beforehand
items.explanation: Students bring it with them, and a random draw leaves it to chance which group it lands in.

items.label: How much each student normally sleeps
items.explanation: It is a trait of the person, so random assignment tends to even it out between groups.

items.label: The score on a second recall test taken a week later
items.explanation: It is a second measure of the effect, taken after the sleep was set.

questions.onCorrect: The researchers set the independent variable and measure the dependent one, while random assignment leaves traits like prior memory to chance, so they tend to even out between the groups.

questions.prompt: Darwin sent queries like these to observers in distant places and asked them to report what they saw. What makes the answers weaker evidence?
hints: Read question (1). Does it let the observer answer without the expression Darwin expects?
Think about what an observer who knew the hypothesis might do without meaning to.

acceptedIdeas: Each question names the expected answer, so a yes is easy to give
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each question names the expected answer, so a yes is easy to give

choices.label: They ask about emotions, which nobody can observe from outside the person
They went to far too few people for any answers to be compared
Each question names the expected answer, so a yes is easy to give

extracts.text: (1.) Is astonishment expressed by the eyes and mouth being opened wide, and by the eyebrows being raised? (2.) Does shame excite a blush when the colour of the skin allows it to be visible?
extracts.who: Charles Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
extracts.when: published in 1872, quoting the printed queries he circulated in 1867
extracts.kind: A scientist's book about a question he gathered observations on by post

questions.onCorrect: Each query states the expression Darwin expected, so a yes can come from expectation as much as from sight. A double-blind design answers that worry by keeping the people who measure unaware of the hypothesis.

misconceptions.feedback: Expressions can be seen and described, and Darwin asked for descriptions of what was seen. The weakness lies in how the questions are worded.
Darwin reports thirty-six answers, and a small sample is a different problem from questions that lead.

questions.prompt: Researchers want to test whether a daily walk lowers resting heart rate. In what order should they do these things?
hints: You cannot assign people until you have recruited them, and you cannot compare groups until the month has run.
Something has to be decided before anyone is measured.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They state the hypothesis and fix the measure first, then recruit volunteers, assign them by a random draw, run the month with measurers who are unaware of the groups, and compare the two averages last.

items: State the hypothesis and decide how resting heart rate will be measured
Assign each volunteer to walking or not walking by a random draw
Run the month, with the people who measure unaware of who is in which group
Compare the average heart rate of the two groups

questions.onCorrect: The measure is fixed before the data exist, assignment follows recruitment, and the comparison comes last because it needs every measurement.

questions.prompt: A lab tests an effect with 20 people per group and finds a significant difference of d = 0.9. Earlier studies with thousands of people put the same effect near d = 0.1. The study is invented. What is the most likely explanation?
hints: Which of the two kinds of study gives the steadier estimate?
Think about which small studies reach significance, and what their estimates look like.

acceptedIdeas: Small studies that reach significance tend to overshoot the true effect
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Small studies that reach significance tend to overshoot the true effect

choices.label: The effect is large, because the result was statistically significant here
Small studies that reach significance tend to overshoot the true effect
The earlier studies must be wrong, because this new result is significant

questions.onCorrect: A study with too few people for a small effect can only be significant if its estimate happens to be too big, which is why striking small-sample results so often shrink when they are repeated.

misconceptions.feedback: Significance says a gap this size is unlikely if there were no effect. It does not say the effect is large, and a small study can reach it only by overshooting.
Thousands of people give a steadier estimate than forty, and the small studies that reach significance are the ones that happened to overshoot.

questions.prompt: Bargh, Chen and Burrows (1996) reported that words linked to old age slowed people's walking. Doyen and colleagues (2012) timed the walking with infrared sensors and found no slowing. A defender says the original must stand because it was published in a respected journal. What is the best reply?
hints: Does the standing of a journal change what the infrared sensors recorded?
Recall the reasons the lesson gave for a result failing to repeat.

acceptedIdeas: A careful repeat that finds nothing counts against the original effect
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A careful repeat that finds nothing counts against the original effect

choices.label: A failed replication shows that the original researchers were frauds who invented it
A careful repeat that finds nothing counts against the original effect
One failed replication proves that the effect does not exist at all

questions.onCorrect: Replication is the test that counts: new participants, the same method and a timer that does not depend on anyone's expectations. A published result is a claim that is still waiting for that test.

misconceptions.feedback: Low power, chance and flexible analysis choices explain a good deal of failed replications, so a failure does not show fraud.
A single repeat shifts the evidence without settling it. What counts is the whole picture, including each study's size and method.

questions.prompt: A manager compares two airport screeners. The first catches 95.4% of the weapons and opens half of the harmless bags. The second catches 50% of the weapons and opens 4.6% of the harmless bags. Both have d′ = 1.68. What should the manager conclude?
hints: Both screeners have the same d′. What does d′ measure?
What happens to the hit rate and the false-alarm rate together when the criterion moves?

acceptedIdeas: They are equally good at it and set the line in different places
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are equally good at it and set the line in different places

choices.label: They are equally good at it and set the line in different places
The first is better at it, because it catches almost every weapon
The second is better at it, because it opens far fewer harmless bags

questions.onCorrect: d′ is the distance between the signal and noise curves, and moving the criterion trades hits for false alarms without changing it. The first screener has set a low line and the second a high one.

misconceptions.feedback: A high hit rate comes from a low criterion as well as from skill, and the first screener also opens half of the harmless bags.
Few false alarms come from a cautious line as well as from skill, and the second screener misses half of the weapons.

questions.prompt: A radiologist reads scans, some of which show a tumour. The cases are invented. Which of the four outcomes is each of these?
hints: Two questions settle it: did she say suspicious or clear, and was a tumour really there?
Being wrong when a tumour is there is a miss, and being wrong when none is there is a false alarm.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The suspicious scan with a tumour and the passed scan of a healthy patient are a hit and a correct rejection. The cleared patient with a tumour is a miss. The healthy patient who is marked suspicious and the harmless cyst are false alarms.

items.label: She marks a scan as suspicious, and it does show a tumour
items.explanation: She said yes and a signal was there.

items.label: She passes a scan as clear, but it shows a tumour
items.explanation: She said no when a signal was there.

items.label: She marks a scan as suspicious, but the patient is healthy
items.explanation: She said yes when only noise was there.

items.label: She passes a scan as clear, and the patient is healthy
items.explanation: She said no when only noise was there.

items.label: She clears a patient who is found to have a tumour a year later
items.explanation: The signal was there and she did not report it.

items.label: She recalls a patient whose follow-up scan shows only a harmless cyst
items.explanation: She reported a signal that was not there.

questions.onCorrect: Each outcome combines what she said with what was true. Hits and correct rejections are the two ways of being right, and misses and false alarms the two ways of being wrong.

questions.prompt: A firm rewards the guard who catches the most thieves. Guard X catches 95% of them and raises a false alarm on 50% of quiet nights (z-scores 1.64 and 0). Guard Y catches 75% and raises a false alarm on 5% (z-scores 0.67 and −1.64). Which guard is better at telling thief nights from quiet nights?
hints: Compare d′ = z(H) − z(FA), not the hit rate alone.
Work out d′ for each guard before you decide.

acceptedIdeas: Guard Y, because d′ is 2.31 against 1.64 for Guard X
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Guard Y, because d′ is 2.31 against 1.64 for Guard X

choices.label: Guard X, because X catches more of the thieves
Guard Y, because d′ is 2.31 against 1.64 for Guard X
Neither, because each guard wins on one of the two rates

questions.onCorrect: For Y, d′ = 0.67 − (−1.64) = 2.31, and for X, d′ = 1.64 − 0 = 1.64. Y separates the two kinds of night better, although X catches more thieves because X shouts so readily.

misconceptions.feedback: X's high hit rate comes with a false alarm on half of the quiet nights. A low criterion raises both rates, so the hit rate alone says little about skill.
Each rate alone can be changed by moving the criterion, so d′ is the fair comparison: it combines them and gives a clear winner.

questions.prompt: A person does four tasks in the order A, B, B, A. How many of these trials are switches?
hints: The first trial is never a switch, because nothing came before it.
Compare each trial with the one just before it.

acceptedIdeas: Two: the second and fourth trials follow a different task
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two: the second and fourth trials follow a different task

choices.label: Three: every trial after the first is a switch, in this sequence
One: the task changes from A to B only once in the sequence
Two: the second and fourth trials follow a different task
Four: every trial is a switch of its own, including the first

questions.onCorrect: Trial two (B after A) and trial four (A after B) are the only changes, so there are two switches and each pays the switch cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Only a trial whose task differs from the one before it is a switch, and the second B repeats the task.
The task changes twice, since it also changes from B back to A on the last trial.
The first trial has nothing before it, so it cannot be a switch, and the second B repeats the task.

questions.prompt: In an illustrative task-switching experiment, 24 people take 650 ms on average on trials that repeat the previous task and 800 ms on trials that switch. The same two tasks appear in both kinds of trial. What does the 150 ms difference show?
hints: The tasks are the same in both kinds of trial, so what differs between them?
Ask whether the extra time follows the task or follows the change of task.

acceptedIdeas: Changing task costs about 150 ms a trial in this group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing task costs about 150 ms a trial in this group

choices.label: Changing task costs about 150 ms a trial in this group
The people were slower at one of the two tasks than at the other
Alternating tasks is faster, because each task feels fresher

questions.onCorrect: The same tasks took longer when they followed a different task, so the extra 150 ms is the switch cost. It is paid again on every switch, which is why many interruptions add up.

misconceptions.feedback: Both tasks appear in both kinds of trial, so the difference follows whether the task changed.
The switch trials are the slower ones, so alternating adds time, which is why grouping like tasks leaves fewer switches to pay for.

questions.prompt: The same eight trials, four of each task, can be arranged in different orders. If every switch adds the same cost, in what order do these four arrangements finish, from quickest to slowest?
hints: Every arrangement has eight trials, so only the switches can make a difference.
Count the changes between neighbouring trials in each row.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AAAABBBB has one switch, AABBAABB three, AABABABB five and ABABABAB seven. With the same trials in each, the arrangement with the fewest switches is quickest.

questions.onCorrect: Total time is the time for the trials plus the time for the switches, so with equal trials the fewest switches finish first. Grouping like tasks saves time and alternating them costs it.

questions.prompt: William James wrote this passage in 1890. Which result of the gorilla film study gives the most direct support to its claim?
hints: The claim is about what is present to the senses and never enters experience. What did the viewers fail to enter into their experience?
Look for a result in which something was fully visible and still went unseen.

acceptedIdeas: Half the viewers who counted passes missed a gorilla in plain view
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Half the viewers who counted passes missed a gorilla in plain view

choices.label: The gorilla was small and dim, so many viewers missed it entirely
The viewers who counted the passes counted them correctly, as they were asked
Half the viewers who counted passes missed a gorilla in plain view

extracts.text: Millions of items of the outward order are present to my senses which never properly enter into my experience. Why? Because they have no interest for me. My experience is what I agree to attend to.
extracts.who: William James, The Principles of Psychology, volume 1
extracts.kind: A textbook of psychology written for students and general readers

questions.onCorrect: James says that millions of items present to the senses never enter experience. The gorilla was present to the eyes of every viewer, yet about half of them had no experience of it.

misconceptions.feedback: The gorilla was on screen for several seconds in the middle of the action, and viewers missed it because their attention was on the count.
A correct count shows how well they did the task. The test of James's claim is what they failed to notice while they did it.

questions.prompt: A manager says her team multitask well, because they answer messages while writing reports and everything gets done. What does the research on switch costs suggest they are really doing?
hints: Ask whether two demanding jobs can run at the same moment, or whether attention moves between them.
Recall how many of Watson and Strayer's 200 drivers showed no cost from doing two demanding things at once.

acceptedIdeas: Alternating between the jobs and paying a switch cost each time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Alternating between the jobs and paying a switch cost each time

choices.label: Doing both jobs at once with no loss, as supertaskers do
Alternating between the jobs and paying a switch cost each time
Saving time, because each job feels fresher after a break

questions.onCorrect: Much of what is called multitasking is fast alternation between jobs, and each switch adds a fraction of a second. The team gets everything done, but more slowly than it would in blocks.

misconceptions.feedback: Only about 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost, so the sensible expectation for any one person is a cost.
Every switch adds time. Grouping like tasks leaves fewer switches to pay for, so the alternating routine is slower.

questions.prompt: A cue becomes three times as variable, so its SD goes from 2 mm to 6 mm. How does its reliability, 1 ÷ SD², change?
hints: Work out SD² before and after, then take 1 ÷ each.
Compare 1 ÷ 4 with 1 ÷ 36.

acceptedIdeas: It falls to one ninth of what it was
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls to one ninth of what it was

choices.label: It falls to one third of what it was
It falls to one ninth of what it was
It stays the same, since the cue's reading has not changed

questions.onCorrect: 1 ÷ 2² is 1/4 and 1 ÷ 6² is 1/36, which is a ninth as large. Because of the square, a modest rise in wobble costs a cue a great deal of weight.

misconceptions.feedback: Reliability uses the square of the SD, so tripling the SD divides the reliability by 3², which is 9.
Reliability describes how steady repeated readings are, so a larger SD means a less steady cue whatever one reading says.

questions.prompt: You expect a pole to be upright. In dim light you glimpse it tilted at 10° but cannot be sure, and in bright light you glimpse it at the same 10° and can be sure. Where does the perceived tilt lie in each case?
hints: Treat your expectation as a cue with its own SD.
A steady cue gets a large weight and a wobbly one gets a small weight.

acceptedIdeas: Close to upright in dim light, and close to 10° in bright light
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Close to upright in dim light, and close to 10° in bright light

choices.label: Close to upright in dim light, and close to 10° in bright light
At 10° in both, since the glimpse is what the eyes report
Close to upright in both, since the expectation came first

questions.onCorrect: The percept is a weighted average of the prior and the glimpse. A poor glimpse leaves the prior heavy, and a clear one leaves it light, so what you see depends on how much you trust each cue.

misconceptions.feedback: Expectation is a cue too. A poor glimpse has a large SD and so a small weight, and the prior pulls the percept towards upright.
A clear glimpse has a small SD, so it outweighs a vague expectation, and the percept lands close to the glimpse.

questions.prompt: William James wrote this as the general law of perception. Which idea from the lesson best describes the part that comes out of our own head?
hints: The part from the object before us is the glimpse. Which cue comes from somewhere else?
James says this part comes from the records of our own past experience.

acceptedIdeas: Expectation from past experience, weighed as one more cue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Expectation from past experience, weighed as one more cue

choices.label: Expectation from past experience, weighed as one more cue
Noise in the senses, which adds random error to every reading
A second sense such as touch, which checks the first one

extracts.text: whilst part of what we perceive comes through our senses from the object before us, another part (and it may be the larger part) always comes (in Lazarus's phrase) out of our own head.
extracts.who: William James, The Principles of Psychology, volume 2
extracts.kind: A textbook of psychology written for students and general readers

questions.onCorrect: James's second part is what the lesson calls the prior: expectation built from everything seen before, which is weighed against the glimpse by its reliability. He added that it may be the larger part.

misconceptions.feedback: Noise is in the readings that come from the object. What comes out of our own head is knowledge and expectation, which the lesson calls the prior.
Touch is another cue from the object before us. James's other part comes from our own past experience, which the lesson calls the prior.

questions.prompt: Hearing places a voice 10° to the right with an SD of 8°, and vision places the moving lips at 0° with an SD of 4°. Where is the voice perceived, and why?
hints: Which cue has the smaller SD, and so the larger weight?
The weights are 1 ÷ 64 and 1 ÷ 16, which is 1 to 4.

acceptedIdeas: Near the lips, at about 2°, because vision is the steadier cue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Near the lips, at about 2°, because vision is the steadier cue

choices.label: Midway at 5°, since each sense gives one reading
At 10°, since hearing is the sense that places voices
Beyond 10°, since two agreeing senses should reinforce each other
Near the lips, at about 2°, because vision is the steadier cue

questions.onCorrect: The weights are in the ratio 1 to 4, so the estimate is (1 × 10° + 4 × 0°) ÷ 5 = 2°. The steadier sense pulls the voice towards the lips.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal weights would give 5°, but hearing's SD is twice vision's, so its weight is a quarter as large.
Here hearing has the larger scatter, so vision takes the larger weight. This is why a ventriloquist's voice seems to come from the dummy.
A weighted average always lies between the readings and never outside them. The two cues here disagree, so the estimate falls between 0° and 10°.

questions.prompt: A reader knows the acronyms BBC, NHS and USA but has never seen the string BBCNHSUSA before. How many chunks does she hold when she remembers it?
hints: A chunk is a unit that you already know.
Which parts of the string does she already know?

acceptedIdeas: Three, since each familiar acronym is one chunk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three, since each familiar acronym is one chunk

choices.label: Three, since each familiar acronym is one chunk
Nine, since the string has nine letters in it
One, since she read it as a single string of text

questions.onCorrect: Chunking uses what is in long-term memory to bind several letters into one unit, so the string costs her three slots, far fewer than nine.

misconceptions.feedback: A reader who knows nothing about the string would hold nine separate letters, but she knows three acronyms and holds each as one unit.
She has not met the whole string before, so there is no single unit for it. The chunks are the three acronyms she already knew.

questions.prompt: Chase and Simon showed chess players a position for a few seconds and asked them to rebuild it. Masters did far better than novices when the position came from a real game, but not when the pieces were set out at random. What does this show?
hints: What was different about the random positions?
If masters simply had a bigger store, would the random positions have hidden their advantage?

acceptedIdeas: Their edge comes from knowing patterns and not from a larger memory
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their edge comes from knowing patterns and not from a larger memory

choices.label: Masters have a larger working memory than novices do, and so recall more
Masters simply paid closer attention to the real positions than novices did
Their edge comes from knowing patterns and not from a larger memory

questions.onCorrect: In a real game the pieces stand in familiar patterns that a master holds as single chunks. In a random arrangement there are no patterns, so masters and novices are both limited to about four chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: Both are limited to about four chunks. A bigger store would help with random positions too, and the advantage vanished there.
Attention alone would help with random positions as well. The advantage disappeared when the familiar patterns did, which points to chunks of knowledge.

questions.prompt: Baddeley and Hitch divided working memory into parts. Which part is doing the work in each of these cases?
hints: Ask whether the task is about sound, about pictures and places, about directing attention, or about tying things into one episode.
The executive stores nothing and only directs. The buffer links the other parts and long-term memory.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deciding to stop rehearsing is the central executive. Repeating a number and hearing a list silently are the phonological loop. Picturing a room and tracking chess pieces are the visuospatial sketchpad. Tying a story to what you know is the episodic buffer.

items.label: Deciding to stop rehearsing a phone number so that you can answer a question
items.explanation: It is a decision about where attention goes, and the executive stores nothing itself.

items.label: Repeating a phone number under your breath
items.explanation: It holds speech-based information by rehearsing it.

items.label: Picturing the layout of a room to plan where a sofa will go
items.explanation: It holds images and positions.

items.label: Tying what you have just heard to what you already know, so a story makes sense
items.explanation: It links information from the other parts and from long-term memory into one episode.

items.label: Keeping a list of words in mind by silently hearing them
items.explanation: The words are held as sounds.

items.label: Keeping track of where the pieces stand on an imagined chessboard
items.explanation: It holds positions in space.

questions.onCorrect: Tasks that use different parts interfere little, and tasks that use the same part interfere a great deal, which is the reason for dividing working memory into parts at all.

questions.prompt: A student must remember the digits 1 4 9 2 1 7 7 6 2 0 0 0. She notices that they are three years she knows well, 1492, 1776 and 2000. What has changed?
hints: Count what she has to hold now, before and after she notices the years.
Does grouping change how many chunks the store can hold, or what goes into each chunk?

acceptedIdeas: The number of chunks she has to hold has fallen from twelve to three
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The number of chunks she has to hold has fallen from twelve to three

choices.label: Her working memory has grown, so it can now hold twelve digits
The number of chunks she has to hold has fallen from twelve to three
The digits are now in long-term memory, so working memory is not used

questions.onCorrect: The twelve digits would have been twelve chunks, far beyond the limit of about four. As three known years they take three slots and leave one spare.

misconceptions.feedback: Capacity stays at about four chunks. Grouping changes how much each chunk holds, and the number of chunks that fit stays the same.
The years she knows are retrieved from long-term memory, but she still holds three chunks in working memory.

questions.prompt: Two memories each have a stability of 2 days when learned. One is reviewed successfully on day 3 and the review multiplies its stability by 2.5. The other is never reviewed. What does the model predict about recall on day 20?
hints: Work out the reviewed memory's new stability.
A larger stability means recall falls to 90% later and the curve is flatter.

acceptedIdeas: The reviewed memory is recalled better, because its stability is 5 days and not 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reviewed memory is recalled better, because its stability is 5 days and not 2

choices.label: The reviewed memory is recalled better, because its stability is 5 days and not 2
Both are recalled equally well, because they started with the same stability
The unreviewed one is recalled better, because nothing disturbed it in the meantime

questions.onCorrect: On day 20 the reviewed memory is 17 days past its review, which with S = 5 gives about 73% recall. The unreviewed memory, with S = 2, is predicted at about 47%.

misconceptions.feedback: The review changed the stability of one of them: 2 × 2.5 = 5 days. Where the memories started does not matter once one has been reviewed.
A successful retrieval strengthens a memory instead of disturbing it, so the reviewed curve is the flatter of the two.

questions.prompt: A card is reviewed successfully on days 2, 7 and 19.5, so the gaps between its reviews are 2, 5 and 12.5 days. Why do the gaps grow?
hints: A review is due when predicted recall has fallen to 90%. What sets how long that takes?
What does a successful review do to stability?

acceptedIdeas: Each successful review multiplies stability, so recall holds up for longer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each successful review multiplies stability, so recall holds up for longer

choices.label: The learner tires of the card and begins to look at it less and less often
Each successful review multiplies stability, so recall holds up for longer
Older memories always fade more slowly whatever happens to them

questions.onCorrect: The stability goes from 2 to 5 to 12.5, and each review is due S days after the last one. A card you know well returns rarely, and one you struggle with returns soon.

misconceptions.feedback: The gaps come from the model's stability, which grows with every successful review whatever the learner feels.
Without a review a memory keeps its stability and its curve. It is the successful retrieval that raises stability.

questions.prompt: Ebbinghaus relearned lists of nonsense syllables after different delays and recorded how much of the first effort he saved. Which statement does this passage support?
hints: Compare what the first hour cost with what the next seven hours cost.
A straight line loses the same amount every hour. Does this passage describe one?

acceptedIdeas: Most of the loss comes early, and later hours add far less
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of the loss comes early, and later hours add far less

choices.label: Memory fades at a steady rate, losing the same amount each hour
Everything learned is gone within a day or so of the learning
Most of the loss comes early, and later hours add far less

extracts.text: One hour after the end of the learning, the forgetting had already progressed so far that one half the amount of the original work had to be expended before the series could be reproduced again; after 8 hours the work to be made up amounted to two thirds of the first effort. Gradually, however, the process became slower so that even for rather long periods the additional loss could be ascertained only with difficulty.
extracts.who: Hermann Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (translated by Henry A. Ruger and Clara E. Bussenius, 1913)
extracts.when: from the discussion of his results, first published in German in 1885
extracts.kind: A laboratory report on memory for lists of nonsense syllables

questions.onCorrect: Half the effort was gone after one hour and two thirds after eight, so the first hour took far more than the next seven together. That steep fall followed by a slow one is the forgetting curve.

misconceptions.feedback: One hour cost half the effort, but the next seven hours added only a sixth more. The loss slows, so the line curves.
The passage says the later loss was hard to detect, and Ebbinghaus reports that about a third was still remembered after 24 hours.

questions.prompt: Source A gives some of Ebbinghaus's results and Source B is his comment on them. What does Source B warn a reader against doing with Source A?
hints: Read the words that describe his results in Source B: special, individual and uncertain.

acceptedIdeas: Treating these percentages as a law that holds for everyone and all material
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treating these percentages as a law that holds for everyone and all material

choices.label: Treating these percentages as a law that holds for everyone and all material
Using the figures at all, since he thought they were worthless
Expecting words with meaning to be forgotten as fast as nonsense syllables

extracts.text: After 24 hours about one third was always remembered; after 6 days about one fourth, and after a whole month fully one fifth of the first work persisted in effect.
extracts.who: Hermann Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (translated by Henry A. Ruger and Clara E. Bussenius, 1913)
extracts.when: from the discussion of his results, first published in German in 1885
extracts.kind: A laboratory report on memory for lists of nonsense syllables

extracts.text: Considering the special, individual, and uncertain character of our numerical results no one will desire at once to know what "law" is revealed in them.
