extracts.when: from the discussion of his results, first published in German in 1885
extracts.kind: A laboratory report on memory for lists of nonsense syllables

questions.onCorrect: Ebbinghaus did not claim a law from one person and one kind of material. Murre and Dros repeated the procedure in 2015 and found the same shape, which is why the shape of the curve carries over and the exact percentages do not.

misconceptions.feedback: He calls the results uncertain and special, and he goes on to fit a rough formula to them. The warning is against calling them a law.
Source B does not mention meaningful material. Its warning concerns how special and individual these particular results are.

questions.prompt: A dog has stopped salivating at a bell after many trials of bell without food. After a rest the bell sounds and the dog salivates a little. What does this show about extinction?
hints: If the learned link had been erased, what would the dog do at the bell?
Ask what the simple rule predicts after a rest, and whether the dog agrees.

acceptedIdeas: Extinction weakens the response without erasing what was learned
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Extinction weakens the response without erasing what was learned

choices.label: The dog was never properly conditioned in the first place at all
The simple rule has been shown to be exactly right every time
Extinction weakens the response without erasing what was learned

questions.onCorrect: The response comes back in part after a rest, which is called spontaneous recovery. The simple rule cannot explain it, which is a reminder that the rule is a model of part of the story.

misconceptions.feedback: The dog salivated at the bell before, so it was conditioned. The return of the response after a rest is a separate effect.
The rule keeps V falling towards 0 on bell-alone trials and predicts no return. Spontaneous recovery is something it cannot explain.

questions.prompt: Which schedule of reinforcement is each of these invented cases?
hints: Ask whether the reward depends on a count of responses or on time passing.
Then ask whether the count or the wait is always the same, or changes around an average.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tailor and the bonus are fixed ratio. The machine is variable ratio. The morning post is fixed interval. The angler and the phone checker are variable interval.

items.label: A tailor is paid for every ten shirts finished
items.explanation: Pay comes after a fixed number of responses.

items.label: A machine pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls, averaging one in twenty
items.explanation: The number of responses varies around an average.

items.label: A letter always arrives in the morning post, so the first check after the post comes is rewarded
items.explanation: The first response after a fixed time is rewarded.

items.label: An angler's first cast after a fish takes the bait, which happens at unpredictable times, lands the catch
items.explanation: The first response after a varying wait is rewarded.

items.label: A salesperson earns a bonus on every fifth sale
items.explanation: The bonus follows a fixed number of responses.

items.label: A person checks a phone for messages that arrive at unpredictable times
items.explanation: The first check after a message arrives is rewarded, and the waits vary.

questions.onCorrect: Ratio schedules count responses and interval schedules count time, and either can be fixed or variable. Variable ratio gives fast, steady responding that is the hardest to extinguish.

questions.prompt: The passage below is Thorndike's law of effect. Which of these cases follows from it, with the right name from the lesson?
hints: The law says a satisfying result makes the response more likely. Which case has that, and what exactly is added or removed?
Negative means something is taken away, and punishment means the behaviour becomes less common.

acceptedIdeas: Praise after a raised hand, which makes it more frequent, is positive reinforcement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Praise after a raised hand, which makes it more frequent, is positive reinforcement

choices.label: A tablet that ends a headache and so is taken again later is positive reinforcement
Praise after a raised hand, which makes it more frequent, is positive reinforcement
A fine for dropping litter that makes it rarer is negative reinforcement

extracts.text: Of several responses made to the same situation, those which are accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction to the animal will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the situation, so that, when it recurs, they will be more likely to recur;
extracts.who: Edward L. Thorndike, Animal Intelligence, chapter 5
extracts.kind: A book reporting experiments on animals and the laws of learning drawn from them

questions.onCorrect: Thorndike's law says that responses followed by satisfaction become more likely. Adding praise raises the behaviour, so it is positive reinforcement. Taking away a headache raises it too, but that is negative reinforcement.

misconceptions.feedback: Something unpleasant is removed and taking tablets becomes more likely, so it is negative reinforcement.
The fine takes away money and the behaviour becomes rarer, which makes it negative punishment.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 10 have a disease and 990 do not. The test detects 90% of the people who have it and wrongly flags 10% of those who don't. Which group is larger among the people who test positive?
hints: Work out how many of the 10 sick people the test detects.
Then work out how many of the 990 healthy people it wrongly flags.

acceptedIdeas: People without the disease, about 99 against 9
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: People without the disease, about 99 against 9

choices.label: People without the disease, about 99 against 9
People with the disease, since the test detects 90% of them
The two groups are about equal, since the test is 90% accurate

questions.onCorrect: The test finds 9 of the 10 sick people and flags 99 of the 990 healthy people, so 99 of the 108 positives are false. A rare condition gives the healthy majority more positives than the sick minority.

misconceptions.feedback: Ninety percent of ten people is nine. A high hit rate applied to a small group gives few cases.
The percentages apply to each group separately, and the counts depend on how many people are in each group, here 10 and 990.

questions.prompt: The same test is used in two places. Among people screened with no symptoms, 1% have the disease and a positive result is right about one time in twelve. Among people at a clinic, 10% have it and a positive result is right about one time in two. Why do positive results differ in value?
hints: The test is identical in the two places. What is not identical?
Think about which group has more true positives to go with its false ones.

acceptedIdeas: More of the people tested at the clinic have the disease to begin with
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More of the people tested at the clinic have the disease to begin with

choices.label: The test itself works better on people who already have symptoms of it
More of the people tested at the clinic have the disease to begin with
Doctors in a clinic are simply better at reading the results

questions.onCorrect: At a 10% base rate there are 90 true and 90 false positives per 1,000 people, and at 1% there are 9 true and 99 false. The base rate changes what a positive result means.

misconceptions.feedback: The hit rate and the false-alarm rate are the same in both places. What differs is the base rate.
Reading ability does not change the counts. A positive result is right more often at the clinic because more of the people tested have the disease.

questions.prompt: A town screens people for a disease, and the numbers are invented. Which of the four quantities is each of these statements about?
hints: Ask which group each statement counts out of: everyone, people with the disease, people without it, or people flagged.
The positive predictive value is counted out of the flagged group alone.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two statements about how many people in the town have the disease are base rates. The two about flagging people who have the disease are hit rates. The flagging of people without it is the false-alarm rate, and 18 of 67 flagged is the positive predictive value.

items.label: 2 in every 100 people in the town have the disease
items.explanation: It is the share of the population with the disease before any testing.

items.label: The test flags 90 of every 100 people who have the disease
items.explanation: It counts the flagged among those who have the disease.

items.label: The test flags 5 of every 100 people who do not have the disease
items.explanation: It counts the flagged among those who do not have the disease.

items.label: Of the 67 people flagged, 18 have the disease
items.explanation: It counts the people who have the disease among the flagged.

items.label: In a second town 20 in every 100 people have the disease
items.explanation: It is again a share of everyone before testing.

items.label: The test correctly flags 18 of the 20 people who have the disease
items.explanation: It counts the flagged among those who have the disease.

questions.onCorrect: Each quantity has a different group underneath it. Only the positive predictive value is counted out of the flagged group, which is the group a person who tests positive belongs to.

questions.prompt: A news story says a new blood test for a cancer is '95% accurate', so a positive result means a 95% chance of having the cancer. Which question should a careful reader ask first?
hints: Does a test's hit rate tell you the chance that a positive result is right?
What other number would you need to count the true and false positives?

acceptedIdeas: How common the cancer is among the people being tested
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How common the cancer is among the people being tested

choices.label: How many people were tested in the study in total, and where
Whether 95% is higher than for other medical tests on the market
How common the cancer is among the people being tested

questions.onCorrect: A positive result is right in proportion to the true positives among all positives, which depends on the base rate. Where the cancer is rare, most positives from even an accurate test can be false.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger sample would make the 95% steadier, but it would not turn a hit rate into the chance that a positive is right.
Comparing tests does not say what a positive result means. That depends on how common the cancer is among the people tested.

questions.prompt: A bat and a ball cost £1.10 together, and the bat costs £1.00 more than the ball. In an illustrative class of 100, 60 students answer '10p' for the ball when asked at once, and 20 answer '10p' when told to check the total first. What does the drop suggest?
hints: What is the ball's price? Test 10p against the total.
Ask what changed between the two groups: the problem, or the instruction to check.

acceptedIdeas: Checking uses slow reasoning and corrects many errors of the quick answer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Checking uses slow reasoning and corrects many errors of the quick answer

choices.label: Checking uses slow reasoning and corrects many errors of the quick answer
System 2 is a separate part of the brain that only some people have in them
Quick answers are right more often than answers that were checked

questions.onCorrect: The ball costs 5p, because 10p would make the bat £1.10 and the total £1.20. The quick answer is the one that springs to mind, and the check is what catches it.

misconceptions.feedback: System 1 and System 2 are labels for two ways of thinking, and everyone uses both.
The figure shows the opposite: fewer students give the wrong quick answer of 10p after they check.

questions.prompt: Psychologists describe fast, automatic judgement as System 1 and slow, deliberate reasoning as System 2. Which is each of these cases?
hints: Ask whether the answer sprang to mind or was worked out.
System 2 takes effort and can test the answer that System 1 gave.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 10p answer, the shark judgement and the pull of the wheel are System 1. Solving the equation, testing the answer against the total and counting the k words are System 2.

items.label: Answering '10p' to the bat and ball problem without checking
items.explanation: The answer springs to mind and is not tested.

items.label: Writing 2x + 100 = 110 and solving it for the ball
items.explanation: It is a deliberate step-by-step working out.

items.label: Judging sharks riskier than drowning after several news reports of shark attacks
items.explanation: It rests on how easily examples come to mind.

items.label: Testing a quick answer against the total in the problem
items.explanation: It is the effortful check that catches the first answer.

items.label: Giving a higher estimate after seeing the wheel stop at 65
items.explanation: The anchor pulls the estimate without any deliberate reasoning.

items.label: Counting the words that begin with k and the words with k in the third place
items.explanation: It replaces ease of recall with an actual count.

questions.onCorrect: System 1 gives the answer that springs to mind, and System 2 can test it if we remember to ask. The labels name two ways of thinking that everyone uses.

questions.prompt: In an invented study, two groups saw anchors of 100 and 500 and gave median estimates of 220 and 340. A reader says the anchors were ignored, because the medians are nowhere near the anchors. What is wrong with that?
hints: Compare how far apart the medians are with how far apart the anchors are.
The anchoring index is the difference in medians divided by the difference in anchors.

acceptedIdeas: The medians still differ by 120 for anchors 400 apart, an index of 0.3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The medians still differ by 120 for anchors 400 apart, an index of 0.3

choices.label: Nothing, since an anchor only counts when the estimate lands on it
The medians still differ by 120 for anchors 400 apart, an index of 0.3
The medians differ by 120, so the estimates followed the anchors completely

questions.onCorrect: The index is (340 − 220) ÷ (500 − 100) = 0.3, so the estimates moved about a third as far as the anchors. That is well above 0, the value for estimates that ignore the anchors.

misconceptions.feedback: An anchor pulls an estimate without having to be matched. The question is whether the medians differ as the anchors do.
Following the anchors completely would mean medians as far apart as the anchors are. This gap is much smaller, so the pull is partial.

questions.prompt: People asked beforehand predicted that hardly anyone would go on to the end in Milgram's study. In his first version 26 of 40 volunteers did. What does the gap between prediction and result show?
hints: Compare what people expected with what the volunteers did.
Ask what a rate from one group of 40 volunteers can and cannot tell you about everyone.

acceptedIdeas: People underestimate how strongly an authority's instructions can pull
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: People underestimate how strongly an authority's instructions can pull

choices.label: People underestimate how strongly an authority's instructions can pull
About 65% of people everywhere would obey in the same way in any setting
The people who made the predictions did so carelessly, without thinking

questions.onCorrect: Almost nobody expected the obedience that Milgram found, so the finding is about how badly people judge the pull of an authority, and the rate itself depends on the setup.

misconceptions.feedback: 26 of 40 is the rate for one group of volunteers under one set of conditions. Milgram's own variations moved it down to 12 of 40.
The result shows that people misjudge the pull of authority. It says nothing about carelessness.

questions.prompt: In Darley and Latané's experiment 85% of students alone left their booth to report a seizure before it ended, 62% with one other and 31% with four others. A writer says 'crowds make people less likely to help'. What is the more careful reading?
hints: The percentages are for each person. What is the chance that someone in the group helps?
Chances that each person acts can fall and still leave more chances overall.

acceptedIdeas: Each person's chance fell, but more people give more chances that somebody acts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each person's chance fell, but more people give more chances that somebody acts

choices.label: The writer is right, since more bystanders always mean less help for the victim
Each person's chance fell, but more people give more chances that somebody acts
The writer is right, since people in groups care less about the victim than people alone

questions.onCorrect: The group's chance depends on both the number of people and each person's chance. The number of bystanders alone settles nothing, which is why evidence from real events matters.

misconceptions.feedback: Each person's chance fell, but the chance that somebody acts is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ, and whether it rises or falls depends on how far each chance falls.
Darley and Latané's account is about felt responsibility spreading out when others could act, and it does not say that people care less.

questions.prompt: One witness helps with probability 0.85. Five witnesses each help independently with probability 0.2. Which situation is more likely to produce help?

acceptedIdeas: One witness, at 85% against about 67% for the five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One witness, at 85% against about 67% for the five

choices.label: One witness, at 85% against about 67% for the five
The five witnesses, since more people mean more chances to help
They are about equal, since five times 0.2 comes to 1

misconceptions.feedback: The chance that all five fail is 0.8⁵, about 0.33, so help comes about 67% of the time, below the lone witness's 85%.

questions.prompt: Le Bon wrote this about crowds in the 1890s. In 2020 Philpot and colleagues studied CCTV recordings of 219 real public conflicts in three cities and found that at least one bystander stepped in during 91% of them. How do the two compare as evidence?
hints: Which of the two is a claim from examples and which is a count of real events?
What does the passage say people do in a crowd, and what did the recordings show them doing?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The passage is a claim about crowds, and the footage counted real events and found help usual

The passage is a claim about crowds, and the footage counted real events and found help usual

extracts.text: Moreover, by the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation. Isolated, he may be a cultivated individual; in a crowd, he is a barbarian--that is, a creature acting by instinct.

citations.claim: A correlation is a tendency for two measures to rise and fall together; it is positive when both rise and negative when one falls as the other rises.
The correlation coefficient r runs from -1 to +1; its sign gives the direction and its distance from zero gives the strength.
Strength depends on the size of r, not its sign, so r = -0.6 is stronger than r = +0.4.
Squaring r gives the share of variation two measures have in common, so r = 0.4 gives 0.16, or 16%.
Squaring r = -0.6 gives 0.36, so 36% of the variation is shared; the sign drops out.
A third variable, here temperature, can drive both measures and produce a correlation that disappears when it is held fixed; OpenStax warns that correlation does not imply causation.
Age can account for a correlation between children's shoe size and reading, as a third variable behind both.
A correlation does not show the direction of cause, so the causal arrow could run from either variable to the other.
A correlation between exercise and mood is compatible with mood leading to exercise, as well as exercise leading to mood or a third variable.
An illusory correlation is the perception that two variables are related when they are not; comparing rates in each group exposes it.
Comparing rates, 6 of 20 full-moon shifts and 30 of 100 other shifts were busy, both 30%, so the remembered link is illusory (illustrative counts).
Population is a confound: a third variable that drives both measures.
Hot weather: it brings more people to the ice-cream van and to the pool.
Stronger: r = −0.6 is further from zero. The minus sign only gives direction.
Shared variance is r² = (−0.6)² = 0.36, so 36%. Squaring removes the sign.
Age drives both measures: older children have bigger feet and better reading.
6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.
Two measures correlate at r = 0.7. What percentage of their variation do they share? r² = 0.7² = 0.49, so 49%.

Towns with more fire engines at a fire record more damage, because larger fires bring more engines and cause more damage. What is fire size in this relationship? Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.
Reverse causation runs the arrow from mood to exercise. Sunny weather would be a confound, and endorphins assume the original direction.
One correlation can arise in three ways, so the number alone never says which. Each case needs its own check: hold the third factor still, look for the opposite arrow, or compare the full counts.
When a lottery decides who gets the app, motivation cannot be what separates the groups, which a larger or tighter survey cannot promise. The next lesson explains why.
When participants choose their own group (self-selection), the groups can differ before the study starts, so a later difference cannot be credited to the treatment.
Volunteers for a programme may already exercise more than non-volunteers, giving the programme group a head start (illustrative figures).
In an experiment researchers manipulate one variable; random assignment gives every participant an equal chance of landing in any condition, and the control group receives no treatment.
Random assignment does not make small groups identical; it ensures only that no trait systematically favours one group, and chance gaps shrink as samples grow.
A small chance gap between randomly assigned groups does not undermine the design.
The independent variable is what researchers manipulate and the dependent variable is what they measure; an operational definition states exactly how a concept is measured.
Resting heart rate, measured after the condition is set, is a dependent variable.
Expectation alone can produce improvement, so a control group receives a placebo with no active ingredient; the active ingredient is credited with the improvement beyond the placebo group's.
In a double-blind design neither participants nor the researchers who measure outcomes know who received the treatment; single-blind designs keep only one party unaware.
A placebo keeps expectation equal in the two groups.
Subtracting the placebo group's improvement from the drug group's gives the improvement attributable to the active ingredient: 12 - 8 = 4 (illustrative figures).
It is a double-blind design: both sides are kept unaware of the conditions.
People who choose a programme can differ from those who don't before it starts, and the gym's records can't show how much of the gap that explains.
A chance age gap between randomly assigned groups does not undermine the design, since no trait is systematically favoured.
It keeps expectation equal, so only the active ingredient differs between the groups.
12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.
A therapy group improves by 15 points and a placebo group by 9 points. How many points of improvement are due to the therapy beyond the placebo response? 15 − 9 = 6 points.
What procedure gives each participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition of an experiment? Random assignment.
The members chose their own group, so the keener, fitter ones were already in the programme group. The gap at the end mixes the programme's effect with that head start, which is self-selection.
The researchers set the independent variable and measure the dependent one, while random assignment leaves traits like prior memory to chance, so they tend to even out between the groups.

Each query states the expression Darwin expected, so a yes can come from expectation as much as from sight. A double-blind design answers that worry by keeping the people who measure unaware of the hypothesis.
The measure is fixed before the data exist, assignment follows recruitment, and the comparison comes last because it needs every measurement.
The standard deviation measures how far scores typically lie from their average; in a bell-shaped distribution about two thirds of scores fall within one SD of the mean.
Cohen's d is the difference between two group means divided by the standard deviation; roughly 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large by Cohen's conventions.
Dividing a 6-point gain by a standard deviation of 15 gives d = 0.4 (illustrative figures).
For equal-sized groups the pooled SD is the square root of the mean of the two variances.
With SDs of 2 and 14 the pooled SD is the square root of 100, which is 10, so d = 8 / 10 = 0.8.

A result is statistically significant when a gap that large would arise less than 5% of the time with no true effect; power is the probability of detecting a real effect, conventionally targeted at 80%.
Small studies chasing small effects have low power, so they often miss real effects and the significant ones tend to overstate them.

The pooled SD is built from variances, so the more spread-out group counts for more.
Many small, low-powered studies of a real small effect mostly miss it, and the significant ones tend to overstate it.
d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.
Two groups have means 24 and 30, both with standard deviation 12. What is Cohen's d? d = (30 − 24)/12 = 0.5.
Using n ≈ 16/d² per group, how many participants per group are needed to detect d = 0.8 with 80% power? 16/0.8² = 16/0.64 = 25 per group.
Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no hormonal effect of power poses in 200 people. The other two statements are mathematical facts.
A study with too few people for a small effect can only be significant if its estimate happens to be too big, which is why striking small-sample results so often shrink when they are repeated.
Replication is the test that counts: new participants, the same method and a timer that does not depend on anyone's expectations. A published result is a claim that is still waiting for that test.
A response to a possible signal is a hit, miss, false alarm or correct rejection; the hit rate is hits over signal trials and the false-alarm rate is false alarms over noise trials.
A miss is silence when the signal was present.
In signal detection theory, noise varies from trial to trial and the signal adds to it, so the two distributions overlap and an observer sets a criterion that cannot remove both errors.
Moving the criterion raises or lowers hits and false alarms together without changing the distance between the distributions.

Sensitivity d' is the distance between the noise and signal distributions in standard deviations, d' = z(H) - z(FA); signal detection theory came from radar engineering and was brought into perception by Tanner and Swets in the 1950s.
With z(H) = 1.28 and z(FA) = -1.28, d' = 1.28 + 1.28 = 2.56; hit rate 0.90 has z about 1.28.
d' = 0.84 - (-0.84) = 1.68 for a hit rate of 0.80 and a false-alarm rate of 0.20.
Criterion location c = -[z(H) + z(FA)]/2 measures bias towards yes (negative) or no (positive), independent of d'.
Costs and rewards shift the criterion without changing sensitivity.
With z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0, c = -0.84, a liberal criterion.
It also increases false alarms: more yes responses when no signal is present.
Guard B: he shouts far more often on thief nights than on quiet nights. Guard A shouts almost whatever happens.
A fire was present and the alarm stayed silent: a miss.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Costs and rewards move the criterion. The curves have not moved, so sensitivity is the same.
An observer's hit rate has z = 1.0 and false-alarm rate has z = −0.5. What is d′? d′ = 1.0 − (−0.5) = 1.5.
d′ is the distance between the signal and noise curves, and moving the criterion trades hits for false alarms without changing it. The first screener has set a low line and the second a high one.
Each outcome combines what she said with what was true. Hits and correct rejections are the two ways of being right, and misses and false alarms the two ways of being wrong.
For Y, d′ = 0.67 − (−1.64) = 2.31, and for X, d′ = 1.64 − 0 = 1.64. Y separates the two kinds of night better, although X catches more thieves because X shouts so readily.
The criterion. Shouting more readily raises hits and false alarms together and leaves d′ unchanged.
Selective attention is the focusing on some stimuli and filtering out of others.
In Simons and Chabris (1999), viewers counting basketball passes often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the players; this is inattentional blindness.

citations.claim: In Drew, Võ and Wolfe (2013), 20 of 24 radiologists missed a gorilla 48 times the size of a typical nodule in a lung scan, and most who missed it looked straight at it; the class count beside it is illustrative.
Task switching produces a switch cost: responses are slower on a trial that switches task than on one that repeats it, and preparation reduces but typically does not remove it.
A switch is a trial whose task differs from the previous trial's task.
AABAB has three switches, so with 400 ms trials and 100 ms per switch it takes 2,300 ms (illustrative values).
ABABABAB has seven switches, so with 600 ms trials and 200 ms per switch it takes 6,200 ms (illustrative values).
Alternating sequences contain more switches than blocked sequences, so they accumulate more switch cost.
Six extra switches at 200 ms each add 1,200 ms (illustrative values).
In Watson and Strayer (2010), 5 of 200 participants showed no performance cost when driving in a simulator while doing a demanding concurrent task; they called them supertaskers.

citations.claim: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.
20 of 24 radiologists (83%) searching for nodules failed to notice the gorilla, and eye-tracking showed most looked directly at it.
Only a change of task is a switch. Two As in a row are not.
What name is given to the phenomenon in which people counting basketball passes miss a person in a gorilla suit? Inattentional blindness.
Trial two (B after A) and trial four (A after B) are the only changes, so there are two switches and each pays the switch cost.
The same tasks took longer when they followed a different task, so the extra 150 ms is the switch cost. It is paid again on every switch, which is why many interruptions add up.
Total time is the time for the trials plus the time for the switches, so with equal trials the fewest switches finish first. Grouping like tasks saves time and alternating them costs it.
James says that millions of items present to the senses never enter experience. The gorilla was present to the eyes of every viewer, yet about half of them had no experience of it.
Much of what is called multitasking is fast alternation between jobs, and each switch adds a fraction of a second. The team gets everything done, but more slowly than it would in blocks.
It has one switch instead of seven, and every switch adds a cost.
Perception organises and interprets sensory input; each sensory cue is noisy, and Helmholtz described perception as unconscious inference.
When vision and touch disagree, observers do not simply pick one or average them; their judgment leans towards the more reliable cue.
Ernst and Banks (2002) found that people weight vision and touch in proportion to their reliability, the inverse of the variance.
Reliability is 1 / SD^2, so tripling the SD cuts it to a ninth.
With SDs of 1 and 3 the weights are 0.9 and 0.1, giving 0.9 x 30 + 0.1 x 36 = 30.6.
Weights 0.8 and 0.2 on readings of 50 and 56 give 51.2.
Independent cues' reliabilities add, so the combined SD is below either cue's; Ernst and Banks (2002) found combined visual-haptic judgments close to this prediction.
SDs of 3 and 4 combine to 1/sqrt(1/9 + 1/16) = 2.4.
Top-down processing is perception guided by knowledge and expectation, as opposed to bottom-up processing from sensory features; here an expectation is treated as a cue weighted by its reliability.
Weights 0.9 and 0.1 on an expected 0 degrees and a glimpsed 10 degrees give 1 degree.

Perception guided by knowledge and expectation, rather than built only from incoming sensory features, is called what kind of processing? Top-down processing: knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived.
Roughly where should your best single estimate of the height land? Closer to 50 mm: your eyes are the more reliable cue, so they should count for more.
Why does the answer land nearer 20 than the midpoint, 25? The steadier cue has the bigger weight, so the estimate leans towards its reading.
What is the combined estimate, in millimetres? Weights 1/4 and 1/16 give vision 0.25/0.3125 = 0.8; estimate = 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 56 = 51.2 mm.
Two independent cues have standard deviations of 6 and 8. What is the standard deviation of their reliability-weighted combination? 1/36 + 1/64 = 100/2304, so the combined SD is 48/10 = 4.8.
1 ÷ 2² is 1/4 and 1 ÷ 6² is 1/36, which is a ninth as large. Because of the square, a modest rise in wobble costs a cue a great deal of weight.
The combined reliability is 1/16 + 1/36, so the combined SD is about 3.3 mm. Every independent cue adds information, which is why the estimate ends up below the smaller SD.
The percept is a weighted average of the prior and the glimpse. A poor glimpse leaves the prior heavy, and a clear one leaves it light, so what you see depends on how much you trust each cue.

James's second part is what the lesson calls the prior: expectation built from everything seen before, which is weighed against the glimpse by its reliability. He added that it may be the larger part.
The weights are in the ratio 1 to 4, so the estimate is (1 × 10° + 4 × 0°) ÷ 5 = 2°. The steadier sense pulls the voice towards the lips.
Closer to the steadier cue's reading, because each cue is weighted by 1 ÷ SD².
Working memory holds and uses information briefly; Miller (1956) put its span at seven plus or minus two items and Cowan (2001) argued the limit is about four chunks.
Working-memory capacity is counted in chunks, meaningful units, not in individual items; Miller introduced the term chunk.
Nine unrelated digits are nine chunks, which is five more than a capacity of four (illustrative).
Chunking organises items into meaningful units using knowledge in long-term memory, so more can be held.
A string of known acronyms is held as one chunk per acronym.

Chase and Simon (1973) found that chess masters recalled real-game positions far better than novices, with the advantage largely disappearing for random positions, and attributed this to chunks of familiar patterns.
A 20-piece position held as 4 chunks averages 5 pieces per chunk (illustrative).
Baddeley and Hitch's model has a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad, with an episodic buffer added by Baddeley in 2000.
The central executive directs attention among the other parts of working memory.
Baddeley (1966) found that lists of acoustically similar words were harder to recall in order in short-term memory, pointing to a speech-based code.
What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called? Chunking: grouping items into units already known from long-term memory.
How many digits exceed the limit? Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.
Switching attention from rehearsing a number to answering a question is the work of the central executive.

Lists of similar-sounding words are harder to recall in order. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model does this point to? The phonological loop stores speech-based codes, so similar sounds interfere with one another.
Which component of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model directs attention and coordinates the other parts? The central executive.
Chunking uses what is in long-term memory to bind several letters into one unit, so the string costs her three slots, far fewer than nine.
In a real game the pieces stand in familiar patterns that a master holds as single chunks. In a random arrangement there are no patterns, so masters and novices are both limited to about four chunks.
Tasks that use different parts interfere little, and tasks that use the same part interfere a great deal, which is the reason for dividing working memory into parts at all.
The twelve digits would have been twelve chunks, far beyond the limit of about four. As three known years they take three slots and leave one spare.
Nothing. It stays near four chunks, and chunking changes how much each chunk holds.
Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows steep early loss then slower loss; Murre and Dros (2015) replicated the procedure with one volunteer and found a similar curve.
In the FSRS model stability S is the interval at which predicted recall falls to 90%; the FSRS-4 form is R = 1/(1 + t/9S), and later versions have a flatter tail.

citations.claim: Roediger and Karpicke (2006): after a week, students who practised recall remembered more of a prose passage's ideas than students who reread it, though rereading did better shortly after study.
56% recall after practising recall against 42% after rereading is a 14-point gap (illustrative values in the pattern of the finding).
Studying in short sessions spread over days, rather than one long session, is called what kind of practice? Distributed, or spaced, practice.
What percentage recall does the curve predict 90 days after learning? t/9S = 90/90 = 1, so R = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5, or 50%.
Why does a larger stability slow forgetting? A larger S makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows slowly and recall stays high longer.

A week after studying, students who practised recall remembered 56% of idea units and students who reread remembered 42%. How many percentage points higher was recall practice? 56 − 42 = 14 percentage points.
Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S) with stability S = 3 days, what percentage recall is predicted 9 days later? t/9S = 9/27 = 1/3; R = 1/(4/3) = 0.75, or 75%.
On day 20 the reviewed memory is 17 days past its review, which with S = 5 gives about 73% recall. The unreviewed memory, with S = 2, is predicted at about 47%.
The stability goes from 2 to 5 to 12.5, and each review is due S days after the last one. A card you know well returns rarely, and one you struggle with returns soon.
Half the effort was gone after one hour and two thirds after eight, so the first hour took far more than the next seven together. That steep fall followed by a slow one is the forgetting curve.

Ebbinghaus did not claim a law from one person and one kind of material. Murre and Dros repeated the procedure in 2015 and found the same shape, which is why the shape of the curve carries over and the exact percentages do not.
The students who practised recall.
In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to elicit a conditioned response; Pavlov's dogs salivated to a conditioned stimulus.
Rescorla and Wagner (1972): associative strength changes on each trial by the rate times the difference between the maximum and the current strength.
With rate 0.3 and maximum 1, V is 0.3 after one pairing and 0.3 + 0.3 x 0.7 = 0.51 after two.

Extinction is the weakening of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is no longer followed by the unconditioned stimulus, and spontaneous recovery is its partial return after a rest; in the Rescorla-Wagner rule the maximum is 0 on cue-alone trials.
With V = 0.5, rate 0.2 and maximum 0, the change is 0.2 x (0 - 0.5) = -0.1, so V becomes 0.4.
With rate 0.5 the strength is 0.5, 0.75, then 0.75 + 0.5 x (0 - 0.75) = 0.375.

Operant conditioning changes behaviour by its consequences: reinforcement increases and punishment decreases behaviour, and positive and negative mean adding or removing a stimulus; Thorndike's law of effect preceded Skinner's work.
Adding a pleasant consequence that raises a behaviour is positive reinforcement.

Fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval and variable-interval schedules produce different response patterns, with variable-ratio behaviour the most resistant to extinction; Ferster and Skinner published their schedules research in 1957.
On a fixed-ratio 5 schedule, 30 responses earn 6 rewards.
On a fixed-interval 10 s schedule with a response every 3 s, rewarded responses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this? Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this? Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).
What is V after two pairings? Trial 1: V = 0 + 0.3 × 1 = 0.3. Trial 2: V = 0.3 + 0.3 × (1 − 0.3) = 0.51.
Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial? Without food the bell predicts nothing, so the maximum is 0 and the change is negative.
Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement? Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.

On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn? Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
Rescorla–Wagner with rate 0.4, maximum 1 and V starting at 0: what is V after two paired trials? 0.4, then 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.64.
Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is most resistant to extinction? The variable-ratio schedule.
The response comes back in part after a rest, which is called spontaneous recovery. The simple rule cannot explain it, which is a reminder that the rule is a model of part of the story.
Ratio schedules count responses and interval schedules count time, and either can be fixed or variable. Variable ratio gives fast, steady responding that is the hardest to extinguish.

Thorndike's law says that responses followed by satisfaction become more likely. Adding praise raises the behaviour, so it is positive reinforcement. Taking away a headache raises it too, but that is negative reinforcement.
Counting people gives natural frequencies: of 1,000 people with a base rate of 2%, 20 have the disease and 980 do not.
With a base rate of 2%, a 90% hit rate and a 5% false-alarm rate, 18 true positives and 49 false positives give 18 of 67 positives (about 27%) correct.
With a 1% base rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, 99 of 990 people without the disease are flagged.

Tversky and Kahneman (1974) report that people judging whether a described man was an engineer or a lawyer gave nearly the same probabilities whether the group was 30 engineers and 70 lawyers or the reverse, neglecting the base rate.
The positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positives.
With 500 people, a 10% base rate, 60% hit rate and 20% false-alarm rate, 30 of 120 positives are true (25%).
With a 1% base rate, 90% hit rate and 10% false-alarm rate, 9 of 108 positives are true (8.3%).
The same test (50% hit rate, 5% false-alarm rate) gives a positive predictive value of 10/59 (17%) at a 2% base rate and 100/140 (71%) at a 20% base rate.
With a 10% base rate, 90 true positives and 90 false positives make half of positive results true.
With 20% blue cabs and a 75%-accurate witness, 150 of 350 'blue' calls are correct (42.9%); the cab puzzle was made famous by Kahneman and Tversky with other numbers.

A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called? Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.
Counting 1,000 people gives 18 who have the disease and test positive among 67 positives in all, a little over a quarter. We'll build that count step by step.
Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease? The question is about someone who tested positive, so the flagged group is the whole of the comparison.
What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place. 9/(9 + 99) = 9/108 = 0.0833, or 8.3%.

20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place. Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

1,000 people are screened for a condition that 2% have. The test misses no cases but gives false positives for 5% of people without it. How many false positives are there? 980 do not have it; 5% of 980 = 49.
A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct? 12/(12 + 36) = 12/48 = 25%.
The test finds 9 of the 10 sick people and flags 99 of the 990 healthy people, so 99 of the 108 positives are false. A rare condition gives the healthy majority more positives than the sick minority.
At a 10% base rate there are 90 true and 90 false positives per 1,000 people, and at 1% there are 9 true and 99 false. The base rate changes what a positive result means.
Each quantity has a different group underneath it. Only the positive predictive value is counted out of the flagged group, which is the group a person who tests positive belongs to.
A positive result is right in proportion to the true positives among all positives, which depends on the base rate. Where the cancer is rare, most positives from even an accurate test can be false.

In Tversky and Kahneman (1974), a wheel of fortune stopped at 10 or 65 and participants then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations; estimates were pulled towards the number.
Median estimates were 25% after the anchor 10 and 45% after 65, a gap of 20 percentage points.
The anchoring index (Jacowitz and Kahneman, 1995) is the difference in median estimates divided by the difference in anchors: 20/55 = 0.36 for the wheel experiment.

200 of 600 words is 33.3% (illustrative counts).
Frederick (2005) used problems with a tempting wrong quick answer to measure cognitive reflection; System 1 and System 2 are labels from Stanovich and West popularised by Kahneman.
Ball x and bat x + 100p give 2x + 100 = 110, so the ball costs 5p, not the intuitive 10p.

After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic? The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.
The group that saw 65 guessed higher, though the wheel was plainly random. The next screens give the numbers.
What does an index of 0.35 say about the anchors? An index between 0 and 1 shows how far the estimates moved, as a share of the anchors' gap.
What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)? (59 − 35)/(80 − 20) = 24/60 = 0.4.

In a sample of 600 English words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter. What percentage start with k? Give one decimal place. 200/600 = 0.333, or 33.3%: words with k third are twice as common, though harder to recall.
Anchors of 10 and 60 produce median estimates of 30 and 40. What is the anchoring index? (40 − 30)/(60 − 10) = 10/50 = 0.2.
A number everyone could see was random still pulled the estimates towards it. The medians differed by 20 points when the anchors differed by 55.
The ball costs 5p, because 10p would make the bat £1.10 and the total £1.20. The quick answer is the one that springs to mind, and the check is what catches it.
System 1 gives the answer that springs to mind, and System 2 can test it if we remember to ask. The labels name two ways of thinking that everyone uses.
The index is (340 − 220) ÷ (500 − 100) = 0.3, so the estimates moved about a third as far as the anchors. That is well above 0, the value for estimates that ignore the anchors.
The availability heuristic.
Conformity is changing behaviour or belief to match a group; confederates are helpers of the experimenter.
72 conforming answers out of 18 x 12 = 216 is 33.3% (illustrative counts).

Across Milgram's variations obedience fell as the victim came closer: 26, 16 and 12 of 40 went to 450 V with the learner in another room, in the same room, and with the hand pressed on a plate.
26/40 = 65% and 12/40 = 30%, a fall of 35 percentage points.

Almost nobody expected the obedience that Milgram found, so the finding is about how badly people judge the pull of an authority, and the rate itself depends on the setup.
The group's chance depends on both the number of people and each person's chance. The number of bystanders alone settles nothing, which is why evidence from real events matters.
